Description: Cellular Jail, located in Sri Vijaya Puram, South Andaman district, is a historic colonial prison and one of India’s most important freedom struggle monuments. Built by the British in 1906, it was used to exile political prisoners during the struggle for independence. Today, it stands as a solemn reminder of India’s fight for freedom.

Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose Dweep, formerly known as Ross Island, is located near Sri Vijaya Puram. Once the administrative headquarters of the British in the Andamans, it is now a popular tourist spot with historic ruins, scenic beaches, and rich history.

Before the infamous Cellular Jail was constructed, this island housed a women’s prison and gallows where freedom fighters and convicts were incarcerated during British rule. It stands as a symbol of colonial oppression and India’s freedom struggle.

Chatham Island, famous for housing the historic Chatham Saw Mill—one of Asia’s oldest and largest, established in 1883. It also features a Forest Museum showcasing the rich timber heritage of the Andamans, along with remnants from World War II.

In the Cellular Jail Museum more than 200 photographs of all freedom fighters who were in the Jail are exhibited. Reports about the atrocities, the Jail authorities used to commit in those days and articles published in national newspapers on the mainland are on display. Certain paintings on the barbarous treatment on the prisoners, utensils, vessels, uniforms etc. of the prisoners used in those days and the tools, machines which the prisoners were made to operate, are all in the museum reminding us the untold sufferings of the freedom fighters Jail. The Cellular Jail was where the British Government used to send the prisoners. The structural speciality of the Cellular Jail is that the whole jail consists of cells. Each cell was meant for one inmate only and hence the name. On the inside walls of the central tower of the Cellular Jail, one can find the names of more than three hundred and thirty six freedom fighters and revolutionaries who were imprisoned in the cellular jail for their patriotic fervor.

Name/Title: Andhra Pradesh- Monument- Buddhist Architecture - Nagarjunakonda
Description: Nagarjunakonda is named after Nagarjuna, a Buddhist monk, who lived here around the turn of the 2nd century AD. A magnificent example of ancient Buddhist architecture the original valley was shifted, as it was at the danger of being submerged under the Nagarjuna Sagar Dam. The valley symbolizes a lost civilization, which flourished thousand years ago. A number of excavations were carried out here, which revealed many Chaityas and Viharas. Buddha statues, relics, stone images, Jataka tales encrypted panels and other items of Buddhist origin were also unearthed during excavations. It is believed that the antique sculptures belong to the Ikshvaku rule. The ruins of a university have also been found at Nagarjunakonda.

Name/Title: Andhra Pradesh- Monument- Buddhist Architecture - Sankaram
Description: One of the most important Buddhist sites in Andhra Pradesh, Sankaram is known for its third and fourth century Buddhist structures. The name Sankaram derives from the term Sangharama. Sankaram is famous for the whole lot of stupas, rock-cut caves, brick-built structural edifices, early historic pottery and Satavahana coins that date back to the 1st century CE. The main stupa here was initially carved out of rock and then covered with bricks. Excavations have revealed several antiquities like seals, inscribed tablets, pots, copper coins mostly of seventh century CE.

One of the most famous monuments of Andhra Pradesh, the Thousand Pillar Temple, is a twelfth century temple located in Hanamkonda, which was built in 1163 CE by the Kakatiya King Rudra Deva, following the Chalukyan style of temple architecture. The star shaped, triple-shrined temple built on one metre high platform is dedicated to Lord Shiva (Rudreswara), Lord Vishnu (Vasudeva) and Surya . The temple is famous for its richly carved pillars, screens and detailed sculptures, perforated stone screens, richly carved icons, meticulously designed pillars. It has a majestic monolithic Nandi in a highly polished black basalt stone and the 1000-pillared hall architecture.

is one of the famous forts of India. The name originates from the Telugu words Golla Konda meaning Shepherds Hill. The origins of the fort can be traced back to the Yadava dynasty of Deogiri and the Kakatiyas of Warangal. Originally a mud fort, it was passed on to the Bahmani dynasty and later to the Qutub Shahis, who held it from 1518 to 1687 CE. The first three Qutb Shahi kings rebuilt Golconda, over a span of 62 years. The fort also has the cannons used in the last siege of Golconda by Aurangzeb, to whom the fort ultimately fell. The huge gates of the fort are decorated with large pointed iron spikes. These spikes prevented elephants from damaging the fort. The fort of Golconda is encircled by a 11-km long outer wall. This was build in order to fortify the fort.

Name/Title: Andhra Pradesh- Monument- Qutub Shahi Tombs
Description: The tombs of the legendary Qutub Shahi kings lie to the north of Golconda, about a kilometre away from Banjara Darwaza of the Golconda Fort. Planned and built by the Qutb Shahis themselves, these tombs are said to be the oldest historical monuments in Hyderabad. They form a large group of tombs and stand on a raised platform. The tombs are built in Persian and Hindu architectural styles using grey granite, with stucco ornamentation, the only one of its kind in the world where an entire dynasty has been buried at one place.

Name/Title: Andhra Pradesh- Fairs and Festivals- Ugadi
Description: Ugadi is the Telugu new year day celebrated on Chaitra Suddha Padyami, the first day of the bright fortnight in the month of Chaitra ( April) There is a strong belief that this day's happenings fore shadow the course of events in the entire year ahead. Everybody in the house gets up early in the morning takes an oil bath and puts on new clothes. Torana, are tied to all the doors of the house. A special preparation called ugadi pachadi (chutney) is a must in very house. Fresh tamarind with fresh water, jaggery, fresh mangoes and fresh margosa flowers form the ingredients of Ugadi Pachadi. The significance of this Pachadi is, the mixture of bitter margosa flowers and sweet jaggery is that life also is a mixture of sorrow and joy. In the evening people gather in temples or in common places. The village purohit worships the new panchangam or almanac. Then he announces the influence of various planets during the new year over the wind, rains and crops, cattle, wealth and human beings.

The Salar Jung Museum is one of the oldest museum that has the largest personal collection of artifacts of Nawab Mir Yousuf Ali Khan Salar Jung III. The museum houses more than 43,000 art objects and 50,000 books in the 38 rooms spread over three floors of the building.It also has a prized collection belonging to different civilizations dating back to the first century. Salar Jung III, the former Prime Minister of the seventh Nizam of Hyderabad, spent a substantial amount of his income for over thirty five years to make this priceless collection. The collections include Indian art, middle eastern, far eastern and european art, along with a rare manuscript section. Indian art includes stone sculptures, a Bharhut rail slab, standing Buddha statue, Ananthasayi Vishnu, red stone sculptures of Kushana period etc;, bronze images dating back to later Pallava and Chola periods, jade carvings, painted textiles, wood carvings, miniature paintings, modern art, ivory carvings, textiles, metal-ware, manuscript, arms and armour etc. middle eastern art contains the collection of carpets, paper (manuscripts), glass, metal-ware, furniture, lacquer etc. from Persia, Arabia, Syria, and Egypt. Collection of far eastern art exhibit porcelain, bronze, enamel, lacquerware, embroidery, painting, wood and inlay work from China, Japan, Tibet, Nepal and Thailand etc. Oil and watercolor paintings form an important part of the European collection. Founders gallery displays personal artifacts, momentos received and portraits of the Salar Jungs and the Nizams. Royal clothes, porcelain and silver bowls, books furniture like the ceremonial throne used by Salar Jung III etc. The museum also has a fine selection of printed and embroidered fabrics in cotton, silk and wool belonging to India. Brocades woven with silver and gold thread, silk saris of south India, Kashmiri shawls, muslin waistcloth, famous phulkari embroidery work from Punjab, appliqué temple hangings from Rajasthan, Zari coats, chikan work from Lucknow etc. are displayed here. There is a marvelous childrens gallery showcasing assemblage of toys from all over the world. It displays puppets, model trains and objects acquired by Salar Jung III during his childhood. European artifacts include the world famous statue of Veiled Rebecca, her face only visible through a marble veil. Another equally famous sculpture is a 19th century double-figure sycamore wood carving done by G.H Benzoni, an Italian sculptor. The painting gallery possesses the works of famous Raja Ravi Varma, Tagores, Chughtai and contemporary artists of Andhra Pradesh and other parts of India. There is a gallery exclusively for display of guns, daggers, shields and swords including that of Mughal emperor Aurangazeb, Tipu Sultan, Mohammad Shah and from the Qutb Shahi period. Selection of Indian miniatures like Mughal, Rajasthani, Pahari and Deccani paintings are also displayed here. An amazing room is the clock room which is one of the best galleries displaying more than 300 clocks in various sizes ranging from Sandiers to modern day huge pieces. There are tiny pieces set in magnifying glasses to huge and stately clocks from France, England, Germany, Italy and Switzerland. An interesting exhibit here is a musical clock from Cook and Kelvy of England with a toy figure of a watchman, who pushes open the door every hour in a great hurry, to beat the melodious gong to indicate time.

This museum in Hyderabad owes its birth, as its name denotes, to the well known collection assembled over forty years by the artist couple, Jagdish Mittal and his wife, Kamla. The Museum's collection specializes in traditional arts and crafts of the Indian subcontinent up to 1900 CE. and consists of around 1580 objects which include: miniature paintings , drawings, manuscripts, calligraphy , bronzes , terracottas and ivory figures ,jade objects, metalware , textiles , arms and armour and artistic handicrafts There are also several select examples of Nepali and Tibetan thangkas . The Museum is particularly rich in miniatures with representative examples, spanning a period from about 1200 CE to the end of the 19th century, including all the important schools like the Western Indian or Gujarati, Rajasthani, Sultanate, Mughal, Pahari or Punjab Hills, Central Indian, and Deccani. All art objects were assembled by the Mittals chiefly for their aesthetic excellence. Some are crucial for scholars since they are the only examples from a particular school. This was because Mr. Mittal is also a serious art historian. It was the dedication of the couple and their almost religious fervour for art collection that such an achievement could have been possible. A large number of art objects of the Museum have been lent for display at the prestigious Festival of India exhibitions held in London ,U.S.A. and France as well as exhibitions held in the National Museum, New Delhi, and Salar Jung Museum, Hyderabad. Medevial 1550-1600 The Charminar constructed in 1591 by Mohammed Quli Qutab Shah was built to mark the end of a plague in Hyderabad city. The city has almost become synonymous with the monument. It is a massive and impressive structure with four minarets around which one finds a fine blend of modernity and tradition. The Charminar is square in shape, each side measuring 100 feet, with a central pointed high arch at the center. It has four imposing arches with a row of small vaulted niches, which face the four cardinal directions. The Charminar is a two-storied building and balconies on the first floor provide a great view of the surrounding areas. A small mosque on the west facing Mecca adorns the top floor of the Charminar. This mosque is said to be the oldest surviving mosque in Hyderabad. The four minarets of the Charminar and their domed finials rising from their lotus-leaves cushion, rise to 180 feet from the ground. The whole structure contains various small and ornamental arches arranged in vertical and horizontal fashion. The projected canopy, decorative brackets and decoration in stucco plaster add graceful elegance to the Charminar. On the upper courtyard, a screen of arches topped by a row of square jalis or water screens provides a delicate look to the Charminar.

Description: The art of floor painting in Andhra Pradesh is known as muggulu. Each day of the week has a selected design or symbol associated with it: shivpith for Monday, kalipith for Tuesday, swastika for Wednesday, Lakshmi for Friday, and so on. The basic motifs include the lotus, the swastika, conch shells, and discs. The Shri figures are very prominent here; Shri is another name for Lakshmi, the goddess of fortune, who is also the goddess of fertility. The lotus appears often, and is depicted differently each time. It appears as a triangular formation, as a magnificent figure in eight petals (ashtadal kamal), and as an elaboration of a conventional motif like the swastika.

Description: Kuchipudi, a blend of music and abhinaya, is Andhra Pradeshs unique contribution to dance which originated from a village called Kuchelapuri or Kuchelapuram in Krishna district around 300 B. A Kuchipudi dancer has to be well versed in dancing, acting, music, various languages and texts. Some of the celebrated performers and gurus were Kuchipudi Brahmins like Lakshmi Narayan Shastri, Chinta Krishna Murti and Vedantam Chinna Satyam.

Name/Title: Andhra Pradesh- Handicrafts- Bidri/Inlay on Metal
Description: The craft of Bidri or inlay on metal originated in Persia. It has motifs of leaves and floral designs of Persian and Mughal art. It was Sultan Ahmad Shah Wali who introduced this craft to India and he and the Nizam of Hyderabad made this craft most popular. Bidriware is a silver inlay work where designs in pure silver are inlaid in an alloy of zinc and copper. Though the original home of Bidri is Bidar in Karnataka, it is perhaps one of the most popular crafts of Andhra. The technique of bidri came to India from Iran (Persia) in the 14th century during the mughal reign when swords and other weapons were decorated with Bidriwork. The designs are drawn free hand using sharp chisels. The base metal (black) is a combination of zinc with copper which are gently heated together. The complex process of Bidriware includes casting, engraving, inlaying and polishing. The items are first cast in moulds made from clay, sand, resin and oil. A simple chisel, of varied shapes and sizes, is then used to engrave the design. Silver metallic wire is then laid in the engraved area. The item is then cleaned and polished to be finally put in copper sulphate solution which gives it the dark colour

Kalamkari refers to a method of painting with natural dyes with a bamboo pen or kalam. Done on cotton or silk fabric, this art flourished at Masulipatnam and Srikalahasti in Andhra Pradesh. The artists use a bamboo or date palm stick pointed at one end with a bundle of fine hair attached to this pointed end to serve as the brush or pen. Vegetable dyes are used on cloth to color the drawings. The dyes are obtained by extracting colours from parts of plants - roots, leaves along with mineral salts of iron, tin, copper, alum, etc., which are used as mordants. The designs are inspired from Hindu mythlogical themes like Ramayana, Mahabharata, Srimad Bhagwat and Puranas. The unique thing about these paintings is that no two panels are similar. The Persian influence on the designs is visible: ornamental birds, flowers, creepers, and mehrabs or archways found chiefly in Mughal architecture are common. In Srikalahasti, outlines are drawn with a pen or quill and fill in the colours through a wax process, and in Masulipatnam the practice is to use wooden blocks carved into designs for printing. Madder and indigo processes are used here and alum is the mordant used to fix the colours. Vegetable dyes in deep rich shades red and blue are used, while green is obtained as a combination of yellow and blue. The washing of the cloth to remove starch and the washing between dyeing and bleaching is done from flowing water of a stream or river. The lines of the design are drawn with a mixture of iron-filings and molasses. The colour schemes used are traditional ones, with women figures in yellow, gods in blue, and demons in red and green. The background colours are usually red with motifs of lotus and other flowers.

Name/Title: Andhra Pradesh- Handicrafts- Leather Shadow Puppets
Description: The shadow play with leather figures is an art form of ancient times. Several families of traditional puppeteers called tolu bommalata conduct these shows for the entertainment by projecting the shadows of these puppets on to a cloth screen. Goat or sheep leather is the main raw material and skin is first stretched tight and is nailed at the corners to keep it intact in the shape. The puppet figure is then traced on the leather and cut out with a very fine chisel. Puppets have all the possible ornaments. Ornaments and clothing are designed by drilling different kinds of holes in the skin. The colours used to paint the leather are obtained from vegetable and mineral sources. To prevent the puppets from twisting a thin strip of smoothened bamboo is fixed firmly and vertically beside the middle on either side.

Name/Title: Andhra Pradesh- Handicrafts- Tie & Dye/ Telia Rumal/ Ikat
Description: Pochampalli in Nalgonda district and Chirala in Guntur district are famous for tie-and-dye weaving. This craft involves a detailed and sophisticated process where the warp and the weft are tied and dyed according to a predetermined design. Both cotton and silk fabrics are prepared using this process. The patola or ikat saris of Pochampalli are generally centered on geometrical designs. A large variety of cotton lungis for men are also prepared using this technique. Telia rumal is a square shaped cloth using the tie-and-dye technique. Pochampalli, Koyalagudeni and Puttupaka villages specialize in this art. The word telia refers to the oily smell imparted by the use of alizarin dyes and rumal means square. Alizarin, iron or indigo and numerous vegetable oils are involved in the making of this cloth. The fabric is oiled and then tied in certain areas to prevent the dye from penetrating. The tied fabric is dipped in the dye. The end product is a soft and shiny cloth featuring intricate designs. The colors, which include red, pink and purple, vary in their intensities depending on the oil mordant that is used. This cloth can be worn as a headgear, stole, lungi and even as sari.

The best known toys with the widest range in Andhra Pradesh are those from Kondapalli, a small village in the Vijaywada district. They are especially made for festivals like Makar Sankranti and Dusshera. The themes are centered around the villages and the different vocations common to rural life. Tella Poniki, a particular variety of soft wood, is used in the making of the Kondapalli toys. The wood is seasoned and cut into appropriate size. Each organ of the body is separately carved and joined together with an adhesive paste derived from tamarind seeds. A coating of white lime is given over the surface. The toy is colored with watercolors using a goat-hair brush. The craftsmen of Nirmal too take advantage of the locally-available soft wood to carve brightly coloured vegetables, fruits and animals. Wooden dolls are made of the soft Poniki or Ankudu wood and Etikoppaka in Visakhapatnam district is another centre that makes exquisite dolls with a rustic touch.

An area that Andhra Pradesh excels is in textiles especially Sarees. Silk and cotton and a mixture of both are used to create beautiful weaves and designs. Pochampalli, Gadwal, Venkatagiri, Narayanpet and Chirala are some of the places where some of the worlds best sarees are woven. Among the cottons, Narayanpet and Venkatagiri are popular. Venkatagiri in Nellore district is known for its excellent cotton sarees with gold borders and large golden pallav. Silk sarees from Dhamavaram are compared with the rich silks of Kancheepuram in broad borders with extensive gold zari work. In Pochampalli sarees of Nalgonda district adjoining Hyderabad, a unique method of tie-and-dye is used and this is known as ikat.

Shilparamam is a crafts village located at Madhapur which is twenty five kilometres from Hyderabad. It was conceived with an idea to create an environment for the preservation of traditional crafts. Annual festivals of arts and crafts are held in March when artisans are invited from all over the country. This helps in establishing a direct contact between the craftsmen and the buyers and also helps in educating people on the value of their rich cultural heritage. Cultural activities are also held during the ten days of Dussehra in October and during the Sankrant Sandadi festival of harvest in January. In order to provide technical advice or any other guidance to craftsmen, the crafts village organizes camps and workshops. A major attraction is the amphitheater where rural and urban artistes meet and interact through workshops, seminars and festivals. Renowned classical dancers and music maestros as well as young artistes come here from all over the country to perform. Folk performances by artistes from the interiors of Andhra Pradesh provide an opportunity to the urban audience to experience the nuances of rural life and culture. Dances like the Koya of the hunting class; Dhimsa, the mild and gentle dance of women; Dappulu, a dance with simple percussion instruments; Veera Natyam, the arduous dance with acrobatic skills and a dozen more are performed. Folk theater and spirited street plays with an element of humor, all add color and represent the primary impulse of the hill folk and tribes.

The Lambadi folk dance, deeply rooted in the cultural heritage of the Lambadi community, carries a fascinating history that spans centuries. This dance form originated from the nomadic lifestyle of the Lambadi people, who have their ancestral roots in Rajasthan, Gujarat, and parts of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana in India. The Lambadi community, historically known as the Banjaras or Gypsies, led a migratory existence, traveling long distances in search of livelihood and trading opportunities. During their journeys, they developed Lambadi folk dance as a means of communication, entertainment, and preserving their cultural traditions.

Some of the important festivals are Mopin of Galos, Solung of Adis, Lossar of Monpas, Dree of Apatanis, Si-Donyi of Tagins, Nyokum of Nyishis, Reh of Idu Mishmis etc. Animal sacrifice is a common ritual in most festivals. There is singing, dancing and animal sacrifices in this five-day festival. 1600-1650 Medieval Tawang Monastery or Gompa is a 400 year old monastery of the Mahayana sect of the Buddhists. Built in the seventeenth century, at a height of 10,000 ft the monastery was founded by a monk called Mera Lama. It is an enormous complex of 65 buildings - a treasure house of old scriptures, priceless images, painted tapestries, books and collection of gold lettered Buddhist scriptures. The Parkhang hall of the monastery houses the library which holds the rare hand written and block-printed Thangkas or manuscripts of revered books like Tangym, Kangyur and Sungbhum. The other rare works of Buddhist literature include 108 gold-embossed manuscripts of the Teaching of Lord Buddha and 225 volumes of the explanations of Buddhas teachings covered with specially designed moth - proof silk adorned with paintings. There is a towering eighteen feet high gilded statue of the Buddha in the monastery complex. Besides the monastery the town promotes the small-scale industries and local handicrafts at their Handicrafts Centre, which has a fine range of woollen carpets and shawls amongst other crafts. Dance is an important part of the lives of the people of Arunachal Pradesh, performed on various occasions such as rituals, festivals and also for recreation purposes. They vary from highly stylised religious dance dramas of the Buddhists to the martial steps and colourful performances of the Noctes and Wanchos. Both men and women take part although there are some dances such as Igu dance of the Mishmi priests, war dances of the Adis, Noctes and Wanchos, ritualistic dance of the Buddhist tribes, which are performed only by male dancers. The Monpas, besides performing Monastic dances for three days during Torgya festivals, also perform other dances on different occasions. Arunachal Pradesh is a land of beautiful handicrafts where people have a tradition of artistic craftsmanship. A wide variety of crafts such as weaving, painting, pottery, basketry, woodcarving etc. are found among the people here.

The craftsmen of Arunachal Pradesh make various cane and bamboo articles for domestic requirements. Bamboo and cane are found in abundance in this region due to the heavy rainfall and temperate climate. The tribal population uses these materials almost exclusively for constructing their dwellings, utensils, furniture, and even weapons such as bows and arrows, spears, armor, and implements like dibbles, hunting and fishing traps. Bamboo and cane are also transformed into colorful basket mats, cane belts, attractive smoking pipes, combs, and a variety of household tools and

One of the important creative activity in the district of Tawang, is the weaving of carpets. A speciality of the Monpas, the Buddhist community, is that it is done mainly by women. The weaving is done with exotic designs of dragons, geometric and floral patterns.

Weaving is an important household industry involving the women of Arunachal Pradesh. The actual weaving is done with a bamboo tube and using cotton and wool. Bark fibres extracted from trees like udal, pudu and grasscloth is also used. The designs are essentially geometric varying from formal arrangement to lines and bands. The colors that are generally used in the weaves are black, yellow, dark blue, green and scarlet - all put together in the most fascinating combinations. , situated in Guwahati on the Nilachal hill, is the important temple of the goddess Kali. Sibsagar, a historical city was the capital of the mighty Ahoms, who ruled Assam for more than six hundred years before the advent of the British. The most remarkable landmark of the town is the 200 year old Sibsagar tank. On its banks are three significant temples - Shivadol, Vishnudol and Devidol which were all built by Queen Madambika, wife of Siva Singha. The Shivadol is believed to be the highest Siva Temple in India, having a height of 104 feet and the perimeter of 195 feet. The temple belongs to the dvaikuta class in Indian temple architecture and consists of two cells  a garbhagriha (sanctum sanctorum) and a mandapa (pillared hall). The majestic shikhara (dome) with fluted vertical lines rises over the garbhagriha. Vishnudol dedicated to Lord Vishnu, has a Shiva lingam in the sanctum sanctorum, which is quite unique.

Every Assamese celebrates the festival of Bihu - there are three other main festivals which are part of Bihu namely Rangali Bihu, Bhogali Bihu and Kangali Bihu. Of all the festivals that are celebrated in Assam, the Bihu festivals are the most important one and is celebrated by all the Assamese people no matter what their caste, creed, religion and faith might be. Spring festival or Rangali celebrated in the middle of March marks the beginning of agricultural season. The Bhogali or the harvesting festival which is celebrated during January is characterized by a community feast, buffalo fight and other such entertainment. Lastly, the Kangali is another version of the festival celebrated in the middle of October marking the completion of sowing and transplanting of paddies. Sattriya comes from Assam and was first performed in monasteries called sattras. It combines strong and gentle movements, and tells stories through realistic actions, like eating, fighting or showing love. Dancers use their upper body for expression and the lower body for rhythm. It was originally performed by male monks called bhokots, but was later opened to women and the general public. The dance includes group patterns like sarpa and performances, such as the sutradhari dance and gopir nach. Dancers train in sixty-four basic exercises called mati-akhora. Costumes are made from Assamese silk called pat, with traditional local designs and ornaments often with a dhoti or skirt, similar to what monks used to wear. There are two main postures—purusha (male) and prakriti (female). (Ref: NCERT Textbook fekr1, Ch. 13) The 64 rituals are performed through ritualistic dance in the Sattaras of Assam.

Sher Shah Suri of the Suri dynasty of Bihar fought with Humayun in Delhi. His mausoleum was built in the middle of a lake in Sasaram by his architect, Aliwal Khan. The tomb is an imposing structure of stone standing and rising from a large stone terrace. This terrace rests obliquely on a platform with a flight of steps leading to the waters edge. The upper terrace is enclosed by a battlemented parapet wall with octagonal domed chambers at four corners. In the middle of the upper terrace stands the building of the mausoleum on a large octagonal chamber surrounded by a wide verandah on all the four sides. Internally, the verandah is covered by a series of 24 small domes. The roof is a pillared cupola adorned by panels of white glazed tiles now much discoloured. The interior of the tomb is sufficiently well ventilated and lighted through large windows on the top portion of the walls fitted with stone jali in varying patterns. The jambs and spandrils of the arch of the mihrab on the western wall were once profusely adorned with verses from the Quran and inscriptions, with glazed tiles of various colours arranged in geometrical patterns and with beautiful floral carvings in stone enclosed in enamel borders. Much of this decoration has already vanished.

Rajgir, known earlier as Rajagriha or Girivaraja, located in the rocky hills is significant for the teachings of both Buddha and Mahavira. Rajgir is 10km south of Nalanda and sacred to the memory of the founder of both Buddhism and Jainism. Lord Buddha spent many months of retreat during the rainy season here, and used to meditate and preach on Giddhkuta, the Hill of the Vultures. Lord Mahavir spent fourteen years of his life at Rajgir and Nalanda. It was in Rajgriha that Lord Buddha delivered some of his famous sermons and converted a number of people to Buddhism including King Bimbisara of Magadha. Today, Rajgir is a picturesque and serene place, visited by pilgrims from all over. Venuvana is the site of the monastery Venuvana Vihar built by King Bimbisara for Lord Buddha to reside. This was the King's first offering to Lord Buddha. Swarna Bhandar are cave chambers which were hollowed out of a single massive rock. One of the chambers is believed to have been the guard room, the rear wall has two straight vertical lines and one horizontal line cut into the rock; this doorway is supposed to lead to King Bimbisaras treasury. Inscriptions in the Sankhalipi or shell script, etched into the wall and so far undeciphered, are believed to give the clue to open the doorway. The treasure, according to folklore, is still intact. The second chamber bears a few traces of seated and standing guards etched into the outer wall.

Vaishali is significant to both Buddhists and Jains. Lord Buddha visited Vaishali more than once during his lifetime. He preached his last sermon here and announced his approaching Mahaparinirvana to his followers. Hundred years after he attained Mahaparinirvana, it was the venue of the second Buddhist council held at the time of king Kalasoka. Two stupas were erected to commemorate this event. Lord Mahavir was born on the outskirts Vaishali at a place called Kundupur in 527 BCE and lived in there till he was 22. Vaishali remains an important pilgrimage for Buddhists and Jains.To commemorate the importance of the site, Emperor Ashoka erected one of his famous pillars. It is made of a highly polished single piece of red sandstone, surmounted by bell shaped capital. A life-size figure of a lion surmounts the top of the pillar. There are some important Stupas here. The Buddha Stupa-I has a plain surface.The exterior of this stupa is now in a dilapidated condition One-eighth of the sacred ashes of the Lord Buddha were enshrined here in a stone casket. Excavation at this site in 1958 led to the discovery of Buddha Stupa-II with remains of another casket containing the ashes of the Lord Buddha.

The founder of Buddhism, Gautama Buddha, attained enlightenment under the sacred Bodhi tree or Banyan tree at Bodhgaya. Bodhgaya is one of the four most sacred pilgrimages for the Buddhists. The other three sacred places of Buddhists are Lumbini (Buddha's place of birth), Sarnath (the site of his first sermon) and Kushinagar (place where he left his body). Buddhists from all over the world visit the holy site of Bodhgaya. They have also built many Buddhist temples at Bodhgaya. The Mahabodhi Temple is located where Lord Buddha got enlightenment. The present Mahabodhi temple was restored around 1880 CE. Besides the main Mahabodhi temple there are several other temples at the place. In the inner sanctuary of the temple there is a huge statue of Lord Buddha. In the center of the temple there is a Shivalinga that was installed around 860 CE. It was under the Bodhi tree that Buddha attained enlightenment. A sapling of the original banyan tree was carried by Ashoka's daughter Sanghamitra to Sri Lanka and planted at Anuradhapura where it exists even now. A cutting from the Bodhi tree of Anuradhapura was planted at Bodhgaya when the original tree died. Vajrasana (the seat of stability) under the bodhi tree is believed to be the same seat where Buddha sat, during his meditation. The stone platform, under the Bodhi tree symbolizes the Vajrasana.

Mithila paintings now better known as Madhubani paintings are an indigenous art form from the Mithila region of north Bihar. Here the women of the village paint figures from themes as varied as the daily life of the people to nature, religion and mythology on village walls to mark the seasonal festivals, special events and marriages. These intricately prepared designed wall paintings are passed on by a mother to her daughter. They are characterized by line drawings based on mythological themes, in bright colours and decorative borders. Traditionally Madhubani paintings were always made with Natural dyes. Black was obtained by mixing soot with cow dung, yellow from turmeric or pollen or lime and the milk of banyan . leaves; blue from indigo, red from the kusam flower juice or red sandalwood; green from the leaves of the wood apple tree; white from rice powder; orange from palasha flowers. Women of this village have been practicing this art form for centuries but it came to the forefront only in the 1960s, when a drought hit the area and people had to think of an alternative non-agricultural source of earning. Selling these traditional paintings on handmade paper was the best alternative. And today they are one of the most celebrated arts of the world.

Nalanda, situated at a distance of 90 km. south east of Patna has ruins of the great ancient university and monastery. It was here that the world's first seat of higher learning, a university was established during the Gupta period. There are many versions of what the term Nalanda means. Nalam means lotus and da means to give. Both combined together, Nalanda means giver of lotus. Since Lotus is supposed to represent knowledge, Nalanda means giver of knowledge. The ruins extend over a large area and represent only a part of the extensive establishment. Nalanda has a very ancient history. It was frequently visited by Lord Vardhamana Mahavir and Lord Buddha in the 6th century BC. Nalanda was the largest residential centre of learning that the world had ever known. The library was located in a nine storied building. Since the time of Buddha, the bhikkus were always encouraged to study the various arts and sciences. Learning was greatly encouraged as it served dual proposes: knowledge and practice. The monks therefore took to learning so that they might practice it and realise Dhamma perfectly and thereby enrich the masses. Nalanda was a flourishing residential university with over 10,000 students and 1500 teachers. The university was marked by a lofty wall and one gate. Hiuen Tsang, the Chinese pilgrim spent three years at Nalanda in seventh century. He has left a detailed note about the university, its curriculum, activities and other accounts. The Tibetan pilgrim Dharmasvamin was here in 1234 and has left a gripping account of the monastery's destruction by the Muslims. The great stupa flanked by flights of steps and terraces, votive stupas and beautiful sculptures gives the glimpse of the past glory that once was Nalanda. Many of the stupas were two or the other on the same spot. The excavation of the Nalanda University archaeological complex shows that the edifices are of red brick and the gardens are beautiful. The buildings are divided by a central walkway that goes south to north, the monasteries or Viharas are east of this central alley and the temples of Chaityas to the west. The Vihara-1 is perhaps the most interesting with its cells on two floors built around a central courtyard where steps lead up to what must have been a dais for the professors to address their students. A small chapel still retains a half broken statue of the Lord Buddha. The enormous pyramidal mass of the temple no.3 is impressive and from its top commands a splendid view of the entire area. It is surrounded by smaller stupas, many of which are studded with small and big statues of the Lord Buddha in various poses or mudras.

Traditionally only those people who were dancers were permitted to make the masks. Originally they were made of wood, later of bamboo, then pumpkin shells and now papier-mâché. These masks are painted mainly with flat transparent shades and the lines are bold and clear. Avoiding the realistic identification the masks take up a symbolic character.

Early Medieval 7-11th Centaury The Maikal mountains are home to the Bhoramdeo temple, which is carved on the rocky stones in the Nagara style. This temple was built around seventh to eleventh century CE. The Bhoramdeo temple has a resemblance with the Sun temple of Konark and the Khajuraho temple. The temple is unique for its architecture. Sir Alexander Cunningham was a British archaeologist and army engineer, had termed it as one of the most beautifully decorated temples seen by him.The main temple here has two parts. One is known as Ishtika made temple and the other is completely stone-carved. This medieval temple has been constructed upon a five feet high sprawling platform including a mandapa, antarala and garbhagriha. The mandapa has a square shape having four pillars in the centre and the rest are in periphery, associated with high roofs. There is a half shelter also on each entrance. In the garbhagriha a Shiva Linga is situated. The outer walls are adorned with the sculptures of Lord Vishnu and his other incarnations, besides those of Shiva, Ganesha etc. The row of idols from top to bottom have a size of one, one and half, and two feet height respectively. The bottom part of the temple has four structures to keep the main body of the temple .The idols of elephants and lions queued up on the top give the temple a decorative look. The main idols in the temple are those of Uma-Maheswar, Nataraj, Narsimha, Vaman, Krishna, Surya, Kaal, Bhairava, Nritya Ganesh, Kartikeya, Tandul, Shivgang, Chamunda, Ambika, Saptamatrika and Laxmi-Naryan. The traces of Ramkatha are also engraved here in stones. Amidst a variety of idols the carnal sculptures of the temple are appreciated for their exquisite carving in different erotic poses, obviously to reflect the lifestyle of those historic periods.

A very ancient town of India, Dantewada derives its name from the capital town of the district, named after the presiding deity of the town Ma Danteshwari. Earlier this town was known as Tarlapal and Dantawali, mention of which can be found on the stone carvings found in the district. A splendid temple of Goddess Danteswari is the highlight of this town. It is one of the Shaktipithas which is visited by devotees from different parts of the country through out the year. Constructed, mainly in the south Indian style (Dravida) architecture, and located at the confluence of the holy rivers Shankini and Dhankini, this temple gives a pleasant feeling of peace and immense satisfaction to the minds of devotees.

This festival is popularly celebrated by the Maria Gonds of Bastar to meet relatives settled in different villages across the state. The tribal Goddess is honored by offering the sacrifice of a goat beneath the sacred village tree. The nights are marked with merriment like singing, drinking and dancing. Madai of Narayanpur in Bastar is famous.

The most important festival in the region is a ten days celebration of Dusshera. This festival is believed to have been originated in the fifteenth century by the fourth Kakatiya monarch, Maharaj Purushottam Deo. Almost all the inhabitants of the state participate in this festival. They celebrate Dussehra as a congregation of Maoli Devi and all her sisters. Numerous pujaris (priests) bring local deities beautifully embellished with vibrant colored flowers to the Danteshwari Temple on rathas (chariots) in Jagdalpur. This festival has an underlying spirit of participation, cutting across caste and creed, which prevails. The Dussehra rath, is always pulled by Maria and Dhruva people. The construction of the rath is always exclusively done by the Saoras every year. The iron nails used in the construction of the wooden rath are made by Lohars (blacksmiths).The ropes for dragging the rath are prepared and supplied by the member of the Parja tribe. The construction of the rath is supervised by the Dhakada. Before using the rath for the ceremony it is always worshipped by the members of the Khaki caste.

Chhattisgarh has a very wide variety of bamboo grown in the state and the craftspersons of the state make excellent bamboo items. Articles for daily as well as decorative use are produced by the local tribal artisans. Some of the well known bamboo products of the state include agricultural implements, fishing traps, hunting tools and baskets.

The craftspeople of Chattisgarh make beautiful decorative wood carvings. The skillful craftsmen of the state carve beautiful wooden ceilings, doors, lintels etc using different kinds of wood like shisham, teak, dhudi, sal and kikar. The craftsmen also make pipes, masks, doors, window frames and sculptures.

Bastar is inhabited by the most exotic tribes of India. It is richly endowed with minerals and forest resources. Bastar is, predominantly, a forest area, and home of Marias and Murias, both extremely colorful and picturesque tribes, who have preserved their ancient culture. The lohars of Kondagaon village in Bastar have been engaged in iron craft for generations and indulge in making of farm implements, lamps and other household objects. The iron objects are made by hammering them into shape; they are not cast or moulded. The hot iron is beaten repeatedly to the desired shape while the unnecessary portion is cut away and filed to remove the sharp edges. Hollow images usually bigger than solid ones are made out of beaten iron sheets, folded, cut, and filed to shape the deepak (lamps), and vertical and horizontal rods or strips. These are ornamented with bird and animal figures that are made separately and later joined together into various types of composite lamps. Depending on the variations in structure and use, there are five types of lamps: laman diya, supali diya, gadli diya, khut diya and viman diya.

Bastar and Raigarh districts of Chhatisgarh create Dhokra crafts from bell metal, brass and bronze. Dhokra essentially refers to the casting of bell metal or bass using the lost-wax technique. In Chhattisgarh, it is the Ghadwa community that is associated with this craft. In local etymology, Ghadwa means to shape or create. A variety of products are crated by the Ghadwas for local use such as images of local gods and deities, vessels, and jewellery. The method of lost wax procedure or cire perdue is used to cast bronze articles. carpenters. Mutni, sooja, pinachaku, hatwani, chimta are few of the tools. Though Dhokra casting is used across the globe, the coiled thread technique is unique to Bastar. The traditional lost wax technique is simple and ideal for use in tribal settings. The craftsman begins by winding a slim thread of wax over the contours of a clay core. It is then thickly coated with fine clay obtained from termite bills, and baked on drying, leaving a narrow vent to melt away the wax. The vacuum created between the core and the clay layer is filled with molten metal, which is then allowed to cool down and solidify. Then the outer clay mould is cracked open, revealing the beauty of the final sculpture. Simple as this whole process seems, it requires great precision and skill. The metal must be able to flow uniformly and freely through the narrow spaces, and replace the wax without forming any bubbles or gaps. Cow dung, paddy husk and red soil are also used in the manufacture of Dhokra artifacts. Of all the raw materials used by the Ghadwas, the most important is beeswax. Besides the essential contouring, wax wires and pieces are also used for decorations required for finishing the artifacts. It is used because of its extraordinarily high plastic content and pliability. Examples of lost wax casting are practiced all over the world, but the coiled thread technique is unique to Bastar. A glance at the traditional baskets provides a clue to its origin. The basket makers would wind grass around a rope, which was then coiled into shape. The same technique was translated into metal only much later, with forest dwellers being dependent on natural product long before they began to use metal. Metal anklets with basket weave motifs, and beautiful containers reminiscent of wicker baskets also point towards such a transition.

Chattisgarh produces excellent quality of silks. Raigarh and Champa are the main silk producing centres.The craftspersons perform traditional and contemporary work. Embroidery is the main attraction on the silk fabrics and there are stitches which are as old as 150 years. Marabhai is one of the traditional embroidery which maintains all its traditional stitches and its a form of hand embroidery. Kosa and Ahimsa are the other most commonly used. The silk thread for the weave is obtained from the jungles of Chhattisgarh without killing the silkworms and involves using crushed and dried Mahuwa seeds to trap the silkworms after the formation of the cocoons.

Performed by shepherd community celebrating Krishna & harvest. Raut dance is a traditional dance of the Yadav community which is performed on Deepawali. In this dance, the Rauts, wearing a special costume, sing and dance in group with stick in their hands in the pathways of the village. After the performance of dance in the house of every householder, they gives blessings to every household by singing songs of blessings. ‘Timki’, ‘Mohri’, ‘Dafda’, ‘Dholak’, ‘Singabaja’ etc. are the main instruments of this dance. ‘Dhohas’ are sung in between the dance. These ‘Dhohas’ are filled with devotion, policy, humor and mythological references. Men are mainly involved in Raut dance but children also eagerly follow them.

Diu is famous for the tortoise shell craft where chiefly trinket boxes are made in combination with bone. The shell surface of the box is covered with intricate designs of bones. The designs include fine geometrical patterns, epic figures and animals fringed by floral motifs. A combination of horns, bone and tortoise shells are alsocombined to make products. Bone is also combined with sandalwood, ebony and tortoise shells to create intricate patterns of fretwork that are mounted or inlaid to make ornate octagonal jewel boxes.

1100-1200 Early Medieval The Qutub Minar, probably a tower of victory started by Qutub-ud-din Aibak during the twelfth century, and completed by Altamash is an interesting mix in Hindu and Islamic styles and each of the original three storeys has different designs. The base storey has alternate angular and circular extensions while those of the second one are round and the third one has only angular flutings. The projecting balconies have a very interesting pattern with an intricate design in which triangular pieces of vaulting spring from the corners. The attractiveness of the balconies is heightened by the bands of deep inscriptions. The complex also houses the Quwwat-ul-Islam Masjid which was erected on the site of a Hindu temple. It has an intricately carved ceiling followed by the spectacular courtyard of the mosque which is lined by the rows of the profusely adorned pillars on both sides. Hindu motifs, like tasseled ropes, bells, tendrils, cows and leaves, are visible all over the mosque. The very first indication of the Islamic character of the building come from the elegant pointed arches with curvaceous and serpentine calligraphy of texts from Quran in Arabic crowning them, towards the west of the mosque. A massive stone screen erected in front of the prayer hall, with a central arch and two similar, though smaller, arches on either side; are profusely carved, crowded with exquisite decorations and is one of the earliest and finest examples of the fusion of Hindu and Islamic art. Alai Darwaza, is the first manifestation of Islamic, architecture and ornamentation has a huge dome with a central knob, pointed arches shaped like horseshoes, and the lotus-bud fringes of the arches. The Darwaza is built of red sandstone with arched openings on all sides. The arch frames are embellished with lotus-bud designs, which are also seen in the perforated screens on the sides of the gate.The gateway is very skillfully decorated withcomplex carvings of the geometric patterns and white marble bands of calligraphy. Apart from Qutab minar, the area also hosts many tombs such as Jamali Kamali Tomb, Sultan Garhi Tomb, Balban Tomb, Madhi Masjid, Palam Mosque and many more.

Feroze Shah Kotla, the palace of Feroze Shah Tughlaq has nothing much that survives, except the Ashoka Pillar, which Feroze Shah Tughlaq had brought from Topra, in Ambala and the ruins of the Jama Masjid and a round step well (baoli), which is two floors deep and has antechambers at each level.

1700-1750 Medieval Shahjahan laid out a new walled city called Shahjahanabad (the present old Delhi) along the Yamuna. It is there he erected a Red Fort similar to Agra, its name attributed to the red sandstone of its walls and adorned it with white marble pavilions including halls of public and private audience (Diwan-i-am where the Emperor would sit on a marbled paneled alcove, studded with gems, and hear complaints of the common people and Diwan-i-khas, where the Emperor held private meetings. This hall is made of marble, and its centre-piece used to be the Peacock Throne, which was studded with rubies and gems and was carried away to Iran by Nadir Shah in 1739. Domed and arched marble palaces, plush private apartments like Rang Mahal, the residence of the Emperors wives and mistresses are also part of this magnificent complex. The Rang Mahal was crowned with gild turrets, skillfully painted and ornamented with a complex assortment of decorated with excellent paintings, gold bordered projections, mosaics of mirrors and the ceiling was made with gold and silverwhich wonderfully reflected in a central pool in the marble floor, a mosque (Moti Masjid) and richly designed gardens. Decorated with gold, precious stones and inlays of pietra dura work, the Red Fort still remains an impressive testimony to the Mughal splendor and might.

Jama masjid, the biggest mosque in India started by Shah Jahan, is built of colossal proportions and has a courtyard, which can accommodate 25,000 devotees at a time. Constructed in sandstone and white marble, it combines the best of Hindu and Muslim styles of architecture, standing on 260 pillars supporting 15 domes at varying elevations. The vast courtyard is flanked by pillared corridors which run all along the courtyard and have domed pavilions in the middle on either side. The prayer hall has a magnificent facade of eleven arches, the central one being higher than the others and serving as the entrance. It is topped off by three magnificent domes which are richly ornamented and have black and white marble stripes.

1550-1600 Medieval Humayuns Tomb, built by his widow Haji Begum in 1564 is one of the most spectacular monument belonging to the Mughal period. A dazzling landmark in the evolution of Mughal architecture in India it is the first Indian building to use the Persian double dome and harmonious proportions. The red sandstone and marble structure is believed to be the inspiration for the designs of Taj Mahal. Standing on a stone platform, surrounded by a garden divided into quadrants by water channels. the plan of the building is simply brilliant and very mathematical. Enclosed by a high wall is a square garden divided initially into four large squares separated by causeways and channels, each square divided again into smaller squares by pathways (Charbagh) which is a typical Mughal garden. The intricate and delicately beautiful lattice work on the tomb remained the trademark of Mughal architecture. On the second storey, a high double dome of marble surmounts the roof with pillared chhatris placed around it.

1500-1550 Proto-historic The Purana Qila (Old Fort) stands on the site where the ancient city of Indraprashtha is believed to have existed. Archaeological excavations have yielded Painted Grey Ware pottery which has been dated to 1000BCE. Similar pottery has been noticed in other sites associated with the epic Mahabharata as well, which seems to prove that this indeed was the place where Indraprastha once flourished. The Old Fort was the citadel of the city of Dinapanah which Humayun started building in 1533 and completed five years later.

A tomb roughly on the plans of Humayuns tomb, though much smaller in scale is the Tomb of Safdarjung. The mausoleum built with red sandstone and buff stone is faced with marble and stands squarely in the middle of a garden which itself is on the pattern of the Mughal Charbagh style.

From the time the East India Companys first envoy stepped into India during Jahangirs rule in 1616 to the time they left in 1947 the British followed various architectural styles  Gothic, Imperial, Christian, English Renaissance and Victorian being the essentials. In 1911 the King Emperor George V passed an order declaring that the capital of British ruled India would be moved from Calcutta to Delhi New Delhi, was made by the British.

1700-1750 Medieval The Jantar Mantar built in 1710 by Raja Jai Singh II of Jaipur in Delhi is an observatory consisting of mason-built astronomical instruments to chart the course of astronomical calculations. Jai Singh, who was a very scholarly king with a very keen interest in astronomy and astrology, had other observatories built in Ujjain, Jaipur, Mathura (which no longer survives) and Varanasi Since independence in 1947, New Delhi in particular has grown tremendously as a city and a number of significant architectural projects have been added to its landscape.

Birla Mandir is the first of the temples built across the country by the industrial family of Birla. Built in 1938, it was inaugurated by Mahatma Gandhi on the condition that people of all castes and especially untouchables would be allowed inside. The temple is designed in the Orissan style, with tall curved towers capped by large amalakas (circular ribbed motif at the summit of a temple tower). The exterior is faced with the white marble and red sandstone and the interior court is overlooked by two-storey verandahs on three sides and has a profusion of sculptures, idols, spires and jalis.

The Baha'i House of Worship also known as the Lotus Temple is designed in the shape of a lotus. Its petals are constructed in concrete but are covered with white marble giving an extraordinary lightness to the structure. Nine pools of water around the structure create the illusion of a lotus floating in water. It belongs to the Baha'i Sect and is dedicated to the oneness of all religions.

The Gyarah Murti is a massive black sculpture in stone made by Devi Prasad Roy Choudhary, it depicts the famous Dandi March led by Mahatma Gandhi in 1931 against oppressive salt taxes imposed by the British regime. Delhi has a variety of museums dedicated to different subjects.

Situated in the historic Red Fort, the Archaeological Museum exhibits objects that date to the Mughal period. On view are manuscripts and firmans that display the fine art of calligraphy. Also on view are paintings, textiles and costumes. The museum also houses relics of the 1857 revolt like maps and weapons.

Teen Murti Bhawan was the home of Jawaharlal Nehru, Indias first Prime Minister. Formerly called Flagstaff House, it used to be the house of the British Commander-in-Chief. This was the residence of Nehru from 1948 till his death in 1964. Having a façade of stone and stucco in an austere classical style, it is preserved as a museum and a library of modern Indian history in memory of Jawaharlal Nehru.

Located on the outskirts of Delhi, the Sanskriti Museum is a treasure house of three museums - Sanskriti Museum of Indian Terracotta, museum of textiles and Sanskriti Museum of Everyday Art. Terracotta displays earthen objects made by some of the finest crafts persons, hailing from different parts of India, using their distinctive traditions and techniques. This complex also has crafts persons, where one can see them at work. It exhibits over 150 terracotta items collected from all over the country. The Sanskriti Museum of Everyday Art was set up to preserve the age-old traditions of India. It has functional items of everyday use, like jars, combs, mirrors, toys and kitchen utensils, on its display.

The National Museum offers a unique insight into the history and culture of India. The museum offers splendid and priceless pieces of Indian art and sculpture that have been arranged in galleries, according to the period to which they belong. It displays a fine collection of fine bronze idols,stone sculptures, textiles, coins and tribal art. The famous sculpture of the Dancing Girl from Mohenjodaro belonging to 2,500 BCE is one of the prized possessions here. A collection of Indian miniature paintings from Mughal, Rajasthani and Pahari schools are also part of the display.

Description: The city was planned systematically, combining twentieth century architecture with that of twentieth centuries older. Sir Edward Lutyens was responsible for the overall plan of New Delhi, and his forte is Rajpath, approached by a 3.2km long road flanked by the imposing buildings of the two Secretariats, built by Herbert Baker. Once known as The Viceroy Palace the Rashtrapati Bhawan, built of brown stone, is truly a befitting home for the President of India and remains Lutyens most significant achievement. It is unquestionably a masterpiece of symmetry, discipline, silhouette, colour and harmony flanked by the two Secretariats and the three buildings together, opens into a huge square called the Viceroys Court where the Jaipur Column stands tall. The Viceroys Court, which frames the main entrance to the house, has lateral entrances on the axis of the Jaipur Column. The main entrance is approached by a broad flight of steps which lead to a 12-column portico. The most outstanding feature of the building is the huge copper dome that rises over a vast colonnaded facade. Beneath the dome is the circular Durbar Hall. The coloured marbles used in the hall come from all parts of India. The columns at the front entrance have bells carved into their capitals. To the west the Bhawan overlooks an enormous Mughal garden designed by Lutyens. Here the principles of hierarchy, order, symmetry and unity are extended from the house into the landscape. A series of ornamental fountains, walls, gazebos and screens are combined with scores of trees, flowers and shrubs. The seat of Indian Parliament, the Sansad Bhawan is a marvellous piece of architecture designed by Lutyens and constructed under the direct supervision of Sir Herbert Baker. Designed as a circular structure, the two semicircular house chambers flank the Central Hall with its impressive dome. The building has a continuous open corridor on the first floor fringed with a colonnade of 144 creamy sandstone pillars. The exterior walls of red sandstone are carved in geometric patterns that echo Mughal jaalis. But it wasnt Lutyens or Bakers who built the rest of New Delhi as it is commonly believed; most if its structures were designed by an unknown Englishman called Robert Tor Tussell, who built Connaught Place, Eastern and Western Courts, Flagstaff House (where Jawaharlal Nehru lived later) and the thousands of public buildings, post offices, officers bungalows and public buildings. India Gate, erected as a memorial in the memory of 90,00 soldiers who laid down their lives during world war I is located at Rajpath, the gateway is 42 m high. Also known as the All India War Memorial, India Gate was designed and constructed by Lutyens. Another additional 13,516 names engraved on the arch and foundations form a separate memorial to the British and Indian soldiers killed on the North-West Frontier in the Afghan War of 1919. Another memorial, Amar Jawan Jyoti is in the form of a flame that burns day and night under the arch to remind the nation of soldiers who perished in the Indo-Pakistan War of December 1971. The entire arch stands on a low base of red Bharatpur stone and rises in stages to a huge cornice.

Name/Title: Goa- Monument- Church-Church of Our Lady of Rosary
Description: The oldest surviving church in Goa is the Church of Our Lady of Rosary in old Goa. A combination of Gothic and Renaissance style specific to Portugal, this church is built on the site of Alfonso de Albuquerque's hill of Victory soon after he conquered Goa in 1510. Dedicated to Our Lady of Immaculate Conception or the Virgin Mary, the huge Convent dating from 1606, was the first Nunnery in Asia. It is believed that St Francis would preach here in the evenings. The almost austere simplicity of the exterior stands in contrast to the rich Gothic decorations of the interiors. The roof of the church is supported by wooden beams. The porch has two stories and the facade has round shaped towers on either side. The decorative motifs of this church include cables and anchors with seashells etc. The interiors of the church reflect the influences of other religions in the decorations. The main altar for instance has cashew, flowers and mango designs. The Baroque Period coincides with the Renaissance period in Europe and also coincides with the arrival of missionaries to Goa including St Francis Xavier. Church building during this time reached a peak with styles and plans that were totally European. The churches of Old Goa including the Basilica of Bom Jesus and the Se Cathedral, and the Church of St Cajetan and the largest of them all, the Augustine Church of Our Lady of Grace, now in ruins, belong to this period and style. The architecture of this period is a mixture of Tuscan, Doric, Ionic and Corinthian styles.

Admired as one of the largest churches in Asia, the Se Cathedral church is an expression of the magnificence of the Portuguese era in Goa. It is dedicated to St. Catherine of Alexandria as Alfonso de Albuquerque conquered Goa on the St. Catherine's day (November 25) in 1510. Even though the original mud and stone structure was built in that year itself, the present Se Cathedral church came up in 1652, after years of laborious craftsmanship. The exterior of the church is a blend of Tuscan and Doric architecture styles of Europe, while the interior is a blend of Mosaic-Corinthian style. The interiors are regal with an imposing principal chapel. There are four chapels on either side of the main altar. Although the main façade of the Se Cathedral was flanked by two bell towers, the one towards the north collapsed in 1776. The remaining tower houses five bells including the Golden bell, named so because bits of gold were mixed with other metals for making the bell.

Name/Title: Goa- Monument- Church- Basilica of Bom Jesus
Description: The Basilica of Bom Jesus, or Infant Jesus, is a Catholic basilica. Declared a world heritage site, Basilica of Bom Jesus stands as a fine example of Jesuit architecture. Famous for housing the mortal remains of St. Francis Xavier, the Jesuit missionary to India and Japan, it is one of the richest churches in Goa. This church is covered with marble and inlaid with precious stones and paintings depicting the life of St. Francis Xavier. The facade of the Basilica is a visual delight showing a combination of Ionic, Doric and Corinthian styles in the columns. The ground floor has three portals, above them are three corresponding long windows and on the second floor are three circular windows. The Church is styled with curves and embellishments and the facade is adorned by pillars and carvings.The roof of the church was originally tiled. St. Francis's body was brought to Goa almost 150 years after his death. It was a gift from Medici, Cosimo III, the Grand Duke of Tuscany. It now lies in an airtight glass coffin, placed inside a silver casket fashioned by a seventeenth century Florentine jeweller. The churches of the Indian Baroque period represent the local contribution to church building in terms of style and design especially designs of the outer facade and the ceiling with inclusion of flowers, tropical motifs etc. The prominent churches of this period include the Church of St Francis of Assisi at old Goa, The Church of Holy Spirit at Margao and the Church of St Ana at Talaulim and The Church of Our Lady of Compassion at Divar.

Name/Title: Goa  Monument- Church- Church of St Francis of Assisi
Description: The Church of the St Francis of Assisi was built by eight Franciscan Friars in 1517. It has carved woodwork, murals with scenes from the life of St Francis and the floor is made mostly of gravestones that date from the sixteenth century. The convent behind this church is now an archaeological museum with portraits of Portuguese viceroys, and sculptures from Hindu temples, amongst other things, on display. The churches of the Rococo period are characterized by their rather small size but with an accent on exquisite and ornate finishing on the inside with local motifs and paintings. Another element was the use of Stucco on the exterior facade. The style reflected to a large extent the relaxation of the religious fervor of the Portuguese. This was also the period of the New Conquests. One of the classical examples of this style is the Church of St. Stephen's at San Estevan near Panaji. Others include the Church of Our Lady of Immaculate conception at Moira, the Church of St Alex at Calangute and the Church of Our Lady of Rosary at Margao.

The latest discoveries in the field of Archaeology have brought to light, the movement of the early man in Goa. A possible land route of entry is believed to being through the area marked as NH-17 or from the Malaprabha  Ghataprabha region (from neighboring Maharastra state). A number of stone tools of an early period have been found in many places such as in the Malangini cave, at the basin of Mandovi at Shirgao, and other places. At the same time, early stone tools have also been discovered in the adjoining regions of the neighboring states of Maharastra and Karnataka i.e. at Malvan and Karwar. Also, evidences of microliths and chalcolithic pottery have been found in Goa.

Among the many and various colorful feasts and festivals that are celebrated in Goa, the Goa Carnival is the most eagerly awaited event. The Carnival is exclusive and unique to Goa, and was introduced by the Portuguese who ruled over Goa for over five hundred years. Although, the three-day festival is primarily celebrated by Christians, it has also adapted Hindu tradition and festivities, western dance forms, and turned into a spectacular event. The carnival is held in February for three days and nights,when the legendary king Momo takes over the state and the streets come alive with music and color.It is a weeklong event of festivity and merry-making, which has been celebrated since 18th Century. The carnival is meant to be for feasting and merrymaking. Huge parades march through the streets with bands, dances and floats in the evenings. The origins of the carnival can be traced to carivals started in the Spanish and Portugese colonies, which were known for their singing and dancing.

Name/Title: Goa- Fairs and Festivals- Feast of St. Francis Xavier
Description: The feast of Saint Francis Xavier is held on 3rd December every year at Velha Goa or Old Goa which is about 10kms east of Panaji. The mummified body of St. Francis Xavier is enshrined in a silver casket in one of the chapels of Basilica of Bom Jesus built in 1605 by the Jesuits. The body of the Saint is exposed to public once every ten years and pilgrims from all over the world come to pay homage. The Relics of the Saint placed in a crystal urn show him to be clad in rich vestments with the coat of arms of the queen of Portugal. By the side is a gold medal and a staff covered in gold and 160 emeralds. On the day of the Feast of St. Francis Xavier, the saint's finger is displayed to the public. The exposition of the body of St. Francis Xavier is held once every ten years.

Shigmo is a social festival in Goa which is like Holi, where a puja of the stems of the betel nut, struck on the ground before the temple is performed and a little grass put at their feet is then burnt. There are a number of dances which are performed.

Name/Title: Goa- Museum- Archaeological Museum and Portrait Gallery
Description: Archaeological Museum and Portrait Gallery is at the Convent of St. Francis of Assisi, old Goa. It has the collection of sculptures covering the period before the arrival of the Portuguese. The main gallery has Hindu statues such as Uma- Mahesh. The portraits of Vasco da Gama and Portuguese Governors are placed on the first floor which provides an interesting study in the evolution of court dresses .The museum also boasts of a large coin collection that traces back the history of Goa. One of the main occupations of the early Portuguese in Goa was building of churches and in fact one of Vasco da Gama's main missions for finding the sea route to India was to seek Christians and spices. Christianity was forced upon by the Portuguese during the period of the Inquisition with wide scale destruction of temples and this continued till the official end of the Inquisition in Goa in 1812. In fact, the first Hindu temple allowed to be constructed by the Portuguese in 300 years was in 1818 at Panaji. With a significant population of Goans being Christians for many generations today, the Church is an important factor in Goa's socio-cultural and religious life. The architecture of Goa's churches have undergone notable changes with the passage of time and the fashion of the era that they were built in.

Mussoll is a folk-play-cum-dance played by the Kshatriyas among the Christians from the two villages of Chandor-Kott and Kouddi in Chandor village. Mussoll used by women folk for pounding rice. The dance is a war dance - a dance of a martial race or caste. From the lyrics of the song, the Mussoll dance commemorates the victory over the Cholas by King Harihara II,son of Bukka I of the Vijayanagarempire at the ancient fort of Chandrapur around 1310CE. Mussoll dance has a constituent symbol, i.e. a bear which is the symbol of Cholas. The Mussoll or pounding pestle used in the dance is made of solid bamboo of about 6-7 feet in length with inserted hawk's bells and is carried only by those who will actually dance.

Goa is rich in pottery which is deep rich red in colour, with a smooth surface, and has a charm and style of its own. A large variety of domestic ware which includes attractive water and flower pots, a wide range of figures and panels are also made including figures of saints and Gods and Godesses and animals, ashtrays and pen holders,etc. These depict an old men or women, mother with a child or two children playing, and a variety of such themes. Borde and Bicholim are two famous centres of earthenware in Goa where both utility cum decorative items are produced by the potters.

Goa has an old and rich tradition of wood carving. After the coming of the Portuguese, this craft was turned largely to a magnificent quality in furniture made in western style. However, oriental designs are used in purely floral, animal and human figures. Main places of production are Verem, Bardez and Cuncolim.

Bamboo craft is one of the traditional crafts of Goa and practiced in almost all parts of the state. Bambaoo craft in Goa was practiced here by the mahars, a community of Goa. Initially they produced utility items required by farmers and fishermen for drying and storing of food grains and selling fish, etc. The range of items produced during that time and still in use in villages include patlo (baskets), valli (used for washing rice and grains), supli (for cleaning rice), mats of different sizes (used also as shades for windows for protection against rain and sunlight) and dali (one of the most important item for farmers for drying food grains; it can also be used as floor coverings).

The craft of sisal fibre craft was brought to Goa by nuns from Kerala. Full of ornamentation and decoration, these are bascially utilitarian objects. Attractive and colourful shopping bags, ladies purses, coasters and wall hangings are made from banana or sisal fiber.

Originally a dance of fisherfolk & women during festivals. The Dekhni dance is a vibrant and graceful traditional Goan dance, often performed during religious and cultural celebrations. It is particularly popular in Goa's Hindu communities and is characterized by its fluid, expressive movements. The dance is usually accompanied by devotional songs sung in Konkani, and the lyrics often revolve around themes of love, devotion, and celebration. Dekhni is typically performed by women, and the dancers wear colourful, traditional attire, including elaborate jewellery. The dance involves intricate footwork and hand gestures, showcasing the elegance of the performer. It is usually performed to rhythmic beats played on traditional Goan instruments, such as the dholak and harmonium. The Dekhni is often seen at festivals, temple events, and during celebrations like the Shigmo festival. Its graceful, storytelling nature makes it an important part of Goa's cultural heritage.

Proto Historic 3000-2500 BCE Dholavira located on the North West corner of the Khadir Island in Kutch was discovered in the year 1967 and the ruins of the settlement found here are believed to be more than 5000 years old. These excavation sites are one of the largest Harappansites in India. The ruins of the ancient town serve as a proof of the fact that there is a connection with Indus valley because a planned city has been excavated, which is built according to a geometric plan. The city is divided into the citadel, the middle town and the lower town. The excavation brought to light the sophisticated urban planning and architecture, and unearthed large numbers of antiquities. It is estimated that Dholavira is even older than the port city of Lothal as the excavations conducted here came up with a number of ancient artifacts, like seals, beads, animal bones, gold, silver, terracotta ornaments and vessels linked to Mesopotamia. There is even evidence that the town was an important trade center between other settlements in Sind, Punjab and Western Asia. The most fascinating discovery of Dholavira is the large inscription, comprising of ten letters in the Indus script. Each letter has been engraved on slices of crystalline material.
