Name/Title: Gujarat- Monument- Step Well- Ruda Baoli- Adalaj
Description: One of the well preserved and intricately sculpted step well is the Ruda baoli at Adalaj, located 12 miles north of Ahmedabad. Octagonal in shape, it has stairways from three sides meeting on a wide landing from where it descends down to the water level. The long flight of steps descend, columns and connecting beams create open structures of increasing complexity; the receding perspectives of columns and cross-beams are particularly striking. Wall niches incorporate miniature pilasters, eaves and roof-like pediments. The decoration of the columns, curved brackets and lintels is highly elaborate with repeated friezes and ornamentation of animal motifs and deities. Ahmedabad in Gujarat, has a rich historical heritage that can be traced back to the ancient times. The city was built in 1411 by Sultan Ahmad Shah. Humayun took over Gujarat in 1534 then lost it and it was reclaimed by Akbar in 1572 and therefore has a legacy of Indo- Islamic architecture. The city was surrounded by walls that still exist.

Name/Title: Gujarat- Monument- Mosque- Siddi Bashir Mosque (Shaking Minarets) - Ahmedabad
Description: Known as Shaking Minaret or Jhulta Minar, this small mosque was constructed by Ahmed Shah II for his mother. When one minaret is shaken the other one begins to vibrate. The vibrations at the base of the tower multiply and get transmitted through air tunnels between the two towers. Amazingly, the connecting passageway between the two minarets, however, remains free of any vibration! It was in the nineteenth century, Monier M Williams, a European Sanskrit scholar who first noticed the minarets shaking. Each minaret is three storied tall with delicately carved stone balconies around each storey. Ahmedabad has many such examples of shaking minarets. The mosque at Raj Bibi once had a pair of shaking minarets. But the British, who were ruling over India at that time, dismantled one minaret in order to study the secret of its construction and the mystery behind the swinging effect. The other such shaking minarets are at the mosques of Jami-Masjid and Bibi-ki-Masjid. Sidi Bashir's minars are all that remain of the mosque popularly named after one of Ahmed Shah's favourite slaves. These are the best existing examples of the shaking minarets- built on a foundation of flexible sandstone.

Name/Title: Gujarat- Monument- Mosque- Jami Masjid- Ahmedabad
Description: The largest mosque in Ahmedabad built by Sultan Ahmed Shah I, the founder of Ahmedabad was Jami Masjid. Built in 1424, it is considered as one of the most superb and imposing structures of its class in the world. It is a massive structure with entrances on three sides- west, south and north. The eastern porches have the mausoleum of Sultan Ahmed Shah I. The mosque, which stands on 260 pillars, is supported by 15 domes arranged symmetrically. A feature of the mosque is the royal gallery with beautiful stonework. The courtyard is surrounded by an enclosed corridor. The mosque shows distinctive blend of Hindu and Jain influence on the Sultanate period architecture. Sculptures on the dome and jalis are the evidence that traditional Hindu craftsmen and architects built it while the columns in the hall within the mosque are in Arabic style.

Name/Title: Gujarat- Monument- Step Well- Dada Harirs Vav- Ahmedabad
Description: The Dada Harir's vav at Ahmedabad, is one of the finest example of the Mughal period. The Dada Harir's vav is modelled on the earlier Mata Bhavani's vav, though it has an additional domed pavilion at the entrance. One striking feature of this vav is the complete absence of figural themes. The motifs in stylized scrollwork that adorn the wall niches are examples of Islamic architecture.

A masterpiece of the Solanki dynasty, the Sun Temple at Modhera is one of the few shrines that are dedicated to the Sun God apart from the one at Konark and Martand. Situated on the banks of Pushpavati river, it was built by King Bhimdev (believed to be the descendant of the lineage of Sun God). The temple has a shrine that is designed in a manner, so that the first rays of the Sun shine on the image of the Lord Surya in the garbhagriha. Though the Temple was plundered by Mahmud Ghazni; the architectural grandeur has still not vanished. Erected on a high platform, the Temple appears majestic with its grand structure and the Toranas leading to the main halls. The exterior walls are engraved with intricate carvings, and every single inch of the structure is covered with the sculptural patterns of Gods, Goddesses, birds, beasts and flowers. The Sun Temple is divided into three parts namely Surya Kund, Sabha Mandap and Guda Mandap. Surya Kund is a deep stepped tank in the front of the temple that was used to store pure water. The devotees used to take a halt here for ceremonial purposes before moving towards the temple. More than 108 shrines mark the steps of this tank including the shrines dedicated to Lord Ganesha, Lord Shiva, Sheetala Mata and many others. In front of the tank, a huge torana (archway) leads to the Sabha Mandap. Sabha Mandapwas the assembly hall where religious gatherings took place. This hall is open from all the four sides and has 52 delicately carved pillars. The intricate carvings depict scenes from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and scenes from the life of Lord Krishna. In order to get into the garbhagriha, one has to cross the passage with pillars and arches. Guda Mandap is the garbhagriha that is supported by a lotus-base plinth. Once, this hall used to house the idol of the Sun God. The designing of the hall was done in a way, so that the idol gets the first glimpse of the Sun at equinoxes. The walls represent the Sun God in his 12 different facets of each month. The carved walls also depict the aspects of human life like the cycle of birth and death.

Palitana temples are considered to be the most sacred amongst all the Jain temples and perhaps the largest cluster of Jain temples anywhere. From the base to the peak of the Shatrunjaya hill, where the temples are located, there are in all 863 temples. The interesting fact is that no one is allowed to sleep overnight including the priest, because the temple city has been built as an abode for the Gods. The temples dedicated to the Jain Tirthankaras were built in two phases-the eleventh and twelfth centuries in the first phase and in the sixteenth century as the second phase. Some of the earliest temples built in the eleventh century were destroyed by Muslim invaders in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. The current temples date back to sixteenth century onwards. The hilltops are bounded by sturdy walls and the temples are grouped into nine enclosures each having several minor temples clustered around a central temple. Like the Jains who prefer the purity of white, their temples too are usually white, a combination of plaster and marble. The temples are elaborately ornamental. Throughout the cluster one can see detailed carvings, beautiful idols and images, jeweled statues and intricate toranas. Among the most important temples here, is the Chaumukh temple with its four-faced deity of Adinath enshrined on a marble pedestal in a shrine open on all four sides. Built in the early seventeenth century, it is planned as a large square subdivided into smaller squares, each structure topped by a dome. The innermost five domes topped squares form a cross and represent the five hills sacred to the Jains. The Adishwar temple is probably the most profusely decorated in Palitana. Its ornate pillars and roofs are decorated with intricately cut marble in the shape of dragons. Near the Adishwar temple is the Muslim shrine of Angar Pir. Childless couples make offerings of miniature cradles at this shrine in the hope of being blessed with children. Other temples worth mentioning are the Sampriti Raj, Kumarpal, and Rampal temples.

There are three main caves which were probably Jain and Buddhist monasteries. Babapyara cave is Jain while the cave in Uparkot Fort and the Kapurkodiya caves are Buddhist. Since they were used for residential purposes of the monks they are very plain and have simple and few carvings. Only the Uparkot cave has ancient carvings on its walls and pillars.

The Archaeological museum at Lothal was set up in 1976 to display the artifacts that were recovered from the excavations conducted from 1952 to 1961 at this site. The museum has three galleries which are treasure houses for beads, terracotta ornaments, replicas of seals, shell and ivory objects, copper and bronze objects, mirrors of bronze and copper, perforated and painted potteries, toy bullock carts and a variety of objects made from stone, shell, and bone and tools and potteries yielded from excavations. The most fabulous are, steatite seals with unicorn motifs and inscription, terracotta seals with elephant motifs, seal, gold necklaces, copper and bronze fish hooks, bangles, perforated jars, painted jars, terracotta bull, horse, model boat, ivory scales and shell compass, chess dices, etc. There are maps and drawings depicting an artists impression of the Harappan town of Lothal. One of the galleries showcases game objects, animal and human figurines, weights, painted potteries, objects recovered from burials and ritual objects, miniature potteries, bricks besides a replica of a joint burial and a scaled plaster of Paris model of the city based on reconstructions made by archeologists.

One of the finest textile museums in the world it is housed in a carved wooden haveli. Located in the Sarabhai Foundation, in Shahibagh the Calico Museum of Textiles, was constructed in 1949. Along with the finest collection of not just textiles and clothes the museum boasts of furniture, temple artifacts and crafts of the country. It has a collection of the finest fabrics spun, woven, printed and painted in different parts of India during the last five centuries. One can see the exquisite designs and artwork in kalamkaris, pichhwais, patolas, bandhnis, floor spreads, tent canopies and precious brocades.It has a collection of marble, sandstone and bronze icons and busts split in two thematic sections- gallery for religious textiles and historical textiles. There are colourful embroidered wall hangings depicting legends of Krishna, cloth decorated with tie and dye, glinting mirror work, screen prints, block prints and intricate embroidery. There is an embroidered tent and the robes of Shah Jahan, along with elaborate carpets and plump cushions that once furnished Muslim palace. Special exhibits include Kashmiri shawls, Kullu embroidery, glittering silk brocades from Varanasi, folk art from the Punjab and masks and large wooden temple rathas from Tamil Nadu. The collection also includes some of the best examples of the Patola saris woven in Patan as well as the extravagant Zari work that gilds saris in heavy gold stitching which weigh almost nine kilos.

is a unique museum located on the outskirts of Ahmedabad city. Established in 1981, this museum exhibits utensils of all shapes and sizes. The exhibits have been collected from all over the country and have been displayed around a simple courtyard. The collection includes pots used for storing water cooking and serving utensils, spoons, rolling pins, tiffin carriers, vessel for churning buttermilk, storage jars, feeding cups for infants and havan kunds too. The collection includes pottery, terracotta and wooden articles as well. The display gives a glimpse into the lifestyle of people of the place they belong to and also the craftsmanship involved.

There are artistic kites, rare kites that have been crafted from more than 400 pieces of paper. It is the second such museum in the world. Bhanubhai Shah, a conoisseur of kites is the brain behind the concept of the museum and he is responsible for designing and donating kites to the museum. garba dances, mirror work and block prints,the kites are of different styles. The kites are made from different materials as well. The materials include paper, cloth, polythene, and nylon. One of the most lavishly designed and decorated kites are the hexagonal Rokoku - beautiful Japanese kites.

Name/Title: Gujarat- Museum- Shreyas Folk Museum  Ahemadabad
Description: A really informative and educational museum located close to the suburbs of Ambavadi near Sabarmati is the Shreyas Folk Museum. This museum displays the colorful and traditional folk arts of Gujarat. From textile and clothing to the decorative crafts, the Shreyas Folk Museum brings out the traditional rustic flavor and cultural heritage of Gujarat. The Museum has an exclusive collection of folk arts and objects which reflect the colorful and traditional heritage of Gujarat and gives an insight into the traditional crafts and technology. The collections reflect many of the traditional and rural communities. These communities belong to different villages of Gujarat and in this museum one can get a glimpse of their exquisite artwork. The communities whose culture and folk art are being researched here are Kathi, Rabari, Rharan, Ahir, Brahmins, Banias, Meghvals, Bharvad, Kanbi, Koli, Mer, Bhansali, Rajputs, Khojas, Vohras, Memons and the Miyanas. One of the unique attractions is a complete skeleton of an elephant which has a height of 3.19m. There is an extensive collection of old coins, weapons, puppets, toys, costumes, masks, musical fountains and animal caparisons which recall the grandeur of the bygone era and projects a vintage charm.

Name/Title: Gujarat- Museum- The NC Mehta Gallery  Ahmedabad
Description: Designed by the famous architect Le Corbusier, the NC Mehta Gallery is one of the museums in Ahmedabad which houses an exclusive range of miniature paintings collected from various parts of India, these miniature paintings are the collections of Late Shri Nanalal C. Mehta who was one of the pioneers of Indian miniature painting and the NC Mehta Gallery, Ahmedabad was named after him. He published several books on Sanskrit and Hindi literature and discovered new documents on Indian paintings. Vasanta Vilasa scroll and Chaurapanchasika are some of the treasured collections apart from miniature paintings that include sacred works, ragmala paintings, royal portraits and different social scenes. The Gallery has examples of Western India and Sultanate School paintings, folios of the Jain Kalpasutra and also the Pre-Mughal style folios. One can see folios of the Hamza-Nama and the Sikander Nama which are two of the famous Persian epics. These miniature paintings were mostly drawn on handmade paper with mineral colors. The aim of the display is to inculcate the love for art and paintings in our society and also for the research and further studies in art work.

An ancient fortified city rich in myth and legend, Junagadh has beautiful shrines of Hindus, Jains and Muslims. Deriving its name from the 'old fort', which circles this medieval town, Junagadh was the capital of the Kshattrapa dynasty. The Girnar Hills that landscape Junagadh are a holy refuge to the Jains. The history of Mount Girnar dates back to the empire of Ashoka, who inscribed 14 edicts on a huge boulder en-route to Mt. Girnar peak. There is a huge boulder, housed in a small roadside building, on which are fourteen rock edicts inscribed by Emperor Ashoka.

Name/Title: Vadodara- Museum- Maharaja Fateh Singh Museum
Description: Maharaja Fateh Singh Museum is a museum situated in a corner of the 750-acre grounds of the Lakshmi Vilas Palace built by Sayajirao III, the highly progressive ruler of the former princely state of Baroda. This used to be the royal school for the children of the family. The works of art belonging to the Royal family are displayed in the museum. The major works of art in this museum are the paintings by European and Indian artists including a collection of the commissioned paintings by Raja Ravi Varma. The collection includes portraits of the Royal family in addition to the paintings based on Hindu mythology for which Raja Ravi Varma was famous. There is a collection of sculptures in marble and bronze. These include copies of great masters in bronze commissioned by the royal family of Baroda. This includes original works of renowned artists like Fellicci, an Italian artist whose works adorn not only the Museum but also the Lakshmi Vilas Palace. Some of Fellici's works can be seen in the Public Park known as Sayaji Garden. The museum has an oriental gallery which houses Japanese and Chinese sculptures, Korean ceramics, Japanese screens, copies of Renaissance masterpieces etc. These works were mainly collected by Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad during his visits abroad.

Description: There are four primary schools of Indian Miniature Paintings - the Rajput, the Mughal, Pahari and the Deccan schools. Miniature Painters used varied substances for coloring their drawings, namely- minerals, vegetables, precious stones, indigo, conch shells, pure gold and silver. The illustrated manuscripts of Jains and Buddhists, and the flowering of the Mughal, Rajput, Pahari and Deccan Miniatures are noted for their meticulous execution and artistic skills. The fine stroke of brushes conveyed the themes from the Ramayana, Mahabharata, Bhagvata Purana, Rasikpriya, Rasamanjiri, etc. The themes have also emerged from the compositions of the great poets like Sur, Keshav, Bihari, Matiram, Dev and Puhukar who wrote great poems like Sursagar, Bihari Satsai, Rasraj, Ashtayam and Rasbeli. There are several themes of different nature. They centered on the love of Radha and Krishna. definite narrative content. These brilliantly illustrated paintings glow as if illuminated from inside. The use of bold contrasts such as red, green, blue yellow is definitely a native influence. Artists belonging to Pahari school of painting used bright colors and depicted themes of love. These Paintings from the Hills, were developed at the Hindu royal courts of Kulu, Guler, Mankot, Nurpur, Mandi, Kangra and Basoholi regions of the North Indian mountain valleys.

Raja Ravi Varma was born on April 29, 1848 at Kilimanoor, a small town in Kerala. His uncle was a well known artist known as Raja Raja Varma who gave him elementary art lessons. He was taken to Thiruvananthapuram in his fourteenth year to stay in the royal palace and learn oil painting. Ravi Varma had many opportunities to discover and learn new techniques and media in the field of painting. His later years spent in Mysore, Baroda and other parts of the country enabled him to sharpen and expand his skills and blossom into a mature and complete painter. He was the first artist to cast the Indian Gods and mythological characters in natural earthy surroundings using European realism. His dazzling oil paintings of Indias ancient glory and his mass reproductions through oleography reached out to the Indian populace in an extraordinary scale at the turn of the twentieth Century. Varma had already made a name for himself as a highly talented painter who had mastered the European painter, the Odore Jensen at the Travancore court. His technique of oil painting observing a visiting Dutch paintings had won prizes at Madras and had been highly appreciated by the British governor too. But Baroda, definitely, was a major turning point in his career. Varma was invited to paint a portrait of the 18-year-old Sayajirao Gaekwad in 1881. The young prince was so happy with the result that he not only commissioned Varma to paint portraits of many of his family members thereafter, but also got him to execute more artistically ambitious works on themes drawn from Puranic legends, Sanskrit classics and mythological epics to decorate the newly built Lakshmi Vilas palace. Varma, was one of the first Indian artist to adopt the style of French and British naturalist painters by adopting devices like the chiaroscuro and dramatic lighting effects in the oil-on-canvas medium. But Varma employed these western techniques to paint purely Indian themes. Episodes from literary and mythological sources like those of Dushyant-Shakuntala, Nala-Damayanti, Radha-Krishna, Harishchandra-Taramati, the Mahabharata and the Ramayana were his favourite subjects.

Proto historic 2500-600 BCE The 4,500-year-old archaeological site of Lothal belonging to the Indus Valley Civilisation was discovered in 1954. Like the cities of Mohenjodaro and Harappa in Pakistan, Lothal too had excellent architecture and town planning. Lothal is prominent as the walled city and as the port from where overseas trade was conducted. The dwellings were constructed with baked bricks and had underground drains as in Mohenjodaro. Lothal, literally means 'the mound of the dead, and the most architecturallysophisticated part is its dockyard, which provided berthing facilities for the ships. Constructed from kiln-baked bricks, the dock comprised a basin. A wide channel was constructed to facilitate entry of ships. Near the dock were warehouses for storage of cargo brought in by the ships. This was probably one of the most important ports on the subcontinent. Lothal was an active business center and had business links with Mesopotamia, Egypt and Persia as the seals discovered at the site suggest. The entire city had a drainage system, well laid-out, paved roads and a bath for every house, some of which were double storied and built on mud platforms. Beads made in the city were quite famous and there is evidence of a bead factory in Lothal. Pottery was another flourishing industry. The ruins of a fire altar suggest that the people of Lothal worshipped the fire god along with the sea god. The unique Harappan system of weights and measures was used in Lothal too. Bricks were in a perfect ratio and the decimal system was used for measuring width.

Patola is the most colourful and elaborate weave with its figured body and the subtle merging of one shade into another. Bandhani, the craft of tie and dye of fabrics is an ancient art practiced in many places in Gujarat and Rajasthan. Jamnagar, Anjar and Bhuj are famous centres of this form of craft. Bandhanis of each of these regions are distinctive in design, technique, and ornamentation. The cloth is folded and dyed and designs are created with the combination of small dots and circles. The borders are broad and are worked both in matching and contrasting colours. Amongst the numerous designs the two important ones are barah bagh or bavan bagh which means twelve gardens or fifty two gardens. It is said that the entire bandhani tradition of this region is manifested in the gharchola, a form of a saree. The making of the gharchola is a complicated and time-consuming process. A starched silk odhni or sari is fixed to a large wooden frame using nails. The sari/odhini, coloured red or green, is divided into a network of squares by rows of white tie-dyed spots or woven bands of zari. Motifs within each compartment range from elephants, parrots, and flowers to dancing girls. Jamnagar has a satiny, silk type of glazed silk on which bandhani is done for blouses, vests and lamp shades.

The oldest centre of crochet lace work in Gujarat is Jamnagar where the women of the Vohra community have been engaged in this art since Aurangzeb's time. They specialize in a particular type of conical cap that is shaped using a mould of conical shape while crocheting. The colours are dark, black and brown with white and look as effective as ikat work.

Kye Gompa built in the fourteenth century, the largest and oldest repository of Buddhist learning in the Western Himalayas in the Spiti region has the appearance of a hill fort. In summer very few of the Lamas are in residence, the majority living in their own villages till winter when they return within the sacred walls. Some 200 or 300 monks reside in this monastery in winter. The Gompa has a narrow passage and a winding flight of steps that leads to the topmost building around an open courtyard. There at the top on a raised platform is the zimchung, the chamber where the incarnate of the lama resides. The gompa is a three storeyed structure one of which is literally a basement.The basement is used as the store which stores the treasures of the monastery  old weapons and other artifacts. The gompa has a valuable collection of ancient Buddhist texts called Kangyur. They are also kept in the basement area in a separate square vault with walls having beautiful religious murals. The ground floor of the gompa has an oblong room used as the du khang. The walls of this room are also highly painted with beautiful murals with themes from the jataka and other popular stories. To the right side of the du khang is the gonkhang, a refectory and other rooms. The cells of the monks are boxlike chambers all around at the lower levels. The gompa is also well known for its priceless collection of ancient thangkas.

Tabo Monastery is the oldest Buddhist Monastery in Spiti Valley. It is also one of the most important Gompa in the entire Tibetan Buddhist world. This is the place where the present Dalai Lama will retire to from his duties. High mountains surround the gompa. It was found by Rinchen Tsangpo in 996 CE.. He brought in Kashmiri artists to decorate this gompa which is second in merit only to the Tholing Gompa in Tibet. It is popularly known as the Gem of the Himalayas and has a preserve of ancient Buddhist legacy and houses some of the most sacred texts of Tibetan Buddhism. It also houses a priceless collection of manuscripts and thangkas. Among its treasures are historical murals depicting tales from the Buddhist pantheon. The old section has 9 temples, 23 chortens, a chamber for monks and another for nuns. Five halls arranged in a row are enclosed within the gompa walls. The colourful murals of Tabo come very close to the pure Indian style identified with the rockcut Ajanta and Ellora caves. The technique required the surface to be coated with several thin layers of lime and yak skin glue. It was then burnished vigorously to provide the ground. Next it was smoothed and freshened with animal fat and butter. Natural vegetable dyes and powdered stone colours were mixed with dzo milk and yak urine for painting. The early Indian style murals used a combination of reds and yellows with little stress on landscaping. The area around the principal figures was filled with smaller divinities. In contrast, the images of Tabo wear a serene smile and halfshut dreamy eyes showing introspective devotion.

The arts and crafts of any region are a reflection of its environment, people and traditions. So it is in Himachal. Weaving, carving, painting, or chiselling  are an intrinsic part of the Himachal life. From the upper reaches of Lahaul and Spiti down to the lowlands of Kangra  life and its shades are woven in, painted on, felt in soulful rhythms or celebrated with joyous abandon, carved in, engraved whether it is in the miniature paintings of Kangra, the thangka of Spiti, or the beautiful shawls of Kullu.

Availability of wood abundantly in its forests makes it used profusely for architecture in Himachal Pradesh. The pine and deodar, besides walnut, horse chestnut and wild black mulberry are used for woodcraft. Wood carvings on domestic items are quite different from those in temples or houses. Prominent amongst these designs are: nagbela zigzag line that combines the serpentine pattern with three or four petal flowers in each side of the line; doria continuous line of flowers; kutheri phoola multi-sided figure, sometimes enlarged and the pattern lid in a jali to serve as a ventilator.Houses in all over the valleys of Himachal are extensively ornamented with carvings  on doors, windows, balcony panels etc. The craft also translates into wooden idols of gods and goddesses in traditional styles. Utilitarian objects crafted in wood can be often found in Pahari homes  these may include rectangular boxes to store grains or ornaments. The Gaddi households in Chamba and Brahmaur are famous for their attractive wooden utensils. Villages of Kinnaur still use wooden household utensils extensively. Intricately carved wooden spinning wheels are also in use.

It is the extreme cold climate of Himachal that necessitated wool weaving. Almost every household in Himachal owns a pit-loom and it is not unusual to find men and women spinning yarn on spindle The best-known woven object is the shawl, ranging from extremely fine pashmina to the coarse desar. Kullu in particular has been famous for its shawls with striking geometrical patterns and vibrant colours  the distinctive feature being stripes running along the edges. Caps of Himachal are of distinctive styles and are different in every part of the state. In Kinnaur, not only shawls, but also saris, trousers and pyjamas are woven in wool. The shawls woven in Rampur, known as Rampur chaddar, are famous for their soft texture and durability. In Chamba district, the weaving assumes a chequered pattern. Besides shawls, carpets and blankets are an essential part of the Himachal lifestyle. Carpets in brilliant colours are woven with a variety of traditional motifs  there are garudas on flowering trees, dragons, swastikas, flutes symbolising happiness or lotus blooms signifying purity. Carpets are woven as furnishing, as saddles for horses and as blankets or chutkas. They are also a part of every brides trousseau.

The Shivalik hills have large resources of fine sandstone, which is highly suited for carving, and has played a vital role in keeping alive the stone carvers craft. Numerous stone temples still dot the Himachal landscape. Kangra, Mandi, Bilaspur, Sirmaur, Chamba and Kullu have been traditional centres for stone carving. The giant monolithic carving of the rock cut temple at Masrur in Kangra has been compared to the Mahabalipuram temples for its daring and detailed, elaborate and delicate chiselling.

Description: is a fifteenth century fort which was the capital of the Bahamani dynasty. It is surrounded by a triple-moated wall, with intricate battlements and an imposing gateway. With its beautifully chiselled temples, this World Heritage Site on the banks of the Malaprabha is reminiscent of the richness of Chalukyan architecture. Pattadakal reached its glory under the Chalukya kings and was once used as a ceremonial centre where kings were crowned and commemorated. It has a cluster of ten major temples, which reflect the maturity of architectural style in the Badami and Aihole regions. At the entrance of the site, are the eight century temples of Jambulinga, Kadasiddeshvara, and Galaganatha with their curvilinear shikaras or spires. The biggest temple, dedicated to Shiva, Virupaksha, has a huge gateway, several inscriptions, and a profusion of friezes from the epics. Facing the temple is a pavilion containing a massive Nandi. The style of the large Virupaksha temple is a forerunner of the Chalukya style.This is the only temple that is still used for worship. Parts of the temple predate the Vijayanagar empire. The temple, with nine storied gopuram towers above the other structure at Hampi. The ceiling of the rangamandapa is beautifully painted with scenes from the Puranas. The Mallikarjuna Temple is similar to Virupaksha Temple, in design but smaller in size.

The ornate Papanatha Temple is yet another impressive piece of architecture, with delicately chiselled ceilings and a sixteenth pillared main hall. It has a large mandapa with a Nandi in the centre. It has a northern style shikhara. The Sangameshwara temple dating from the reign of King Vijayaditya (696-733 AD) is the earliest temple in this complex. It is built in a Dravidian style architecture similar to Pallava dynasty architecture of Kanchipuram.

Halebid, the ancient capital of the Hoysalas was earlier known as Dvarsamudra. The Hoysaleswara temple, perched on a star-shaped base amidst lawns, is a sculptural extravaganza. It reflects the Hoysala style in all its grandeur. Its walls are richly carved with an endless variety of Hindu deities, sages, stylised animals, birds, and friezes depicting the life of the Hoysala kings. The temple platform is carved in horizontal bands. Musicians, animals, mythical beasts and humans, have all been sculpted in a row above another band of sculptures in the same way. Even the eaves are densely carved. The tower over the vimana is broken. The temple has one Shiva shrine and another dedicated to Santaleswara, two mandapas and two Nandi shrines.

Badami is situated at the mouth of a ravine between two rocky hills. The exquisite sculptures and the red sandstone cliffs of Badami boast of the four ancient rock-cut caves on top of a hill. They are filled with carved pillars and bracket figures. The largest of them is the third cave, dedicated to Lord Vishnu. The sculptural wonder here is the eighteen-armed Nataraja striking eighty one dance poses in the first cave overlooking the caves is the Agastya Teertha Tank. Its banks are dotted with a cluster of Bhoothanatha temples.

Aihole is considered as the cradle of Hindu temple architecture. There are hundreds of temples in the villages and fields nearby. Durga temple is the most impressive one with its semicircular apse, elevated plinth, and the gallery encircling the sanctum. The Ladkhan Temple, which is one of the earliest temples, was originally a royal assembly hall and marriage mandapa chosen as the abode of a Muslim prince, Lad Khan. The Huchimalli temple with a sculpture of Vishnu sitting atop a large cobra, the Ravanphadi cave temple celebrating the many forms of Shiva, the Konti temple complex, the Umamaheswari temple, the Jain Meguti Temple, and the two-storied Buddhist Temple are the other noteworthy monuments.

Lakkundi has fifty stunning temples and twenty nine inscriptions dating back to the Chalukya period. The most ornate and spectacular of these is the Kashi Vishwanatha temple. The Jain temple dedicated to Mahavira is one of the largest and oldest shrines here. Lakkundi is also noted for its step wells, artistically built with small, canopied niches inside the walls of several wells that enshrine lingas.

The one-time capital of the Adil Shahi kings (1489-1686) is filled with mosques, mausoleums, palaces, forts, watchtowers, and strong gateways, with the massive Gol Gumbaz dominating the landscape. One of the most impressive architectural achievements of the Deccan, is the mausoleum of Muhammad Adil Shah. The tomb is set in a large walled garden, in the Persian style. This path bisects the garden. On either side are ruins of buildings made of dark bricks. This magnificent mausoleum of Mohammed Adil houses the world's second largest dome. Unsupported by pillars it is an architectural wonder. Built in 1659, its most striking features are the seven storied octagonal pillars at the four corners and the heavy bracketed cornice bellow the parapet. The Gol Gumbaz is an enormous cube of stone and masonry. The amazing whispering gallery distinctly echos the faintiest whisper eleven times.

Situated in the village of Somnathpur, the exquisitely carved, star-shaped temple with triple towers is a perfect example of Hoysala architecture. This place boasts of one of the last and the grandest of Hoysala monuments - the Kesava temple. By the year 1268 CE, the year in which the Kesava temple at Somnathpur was built. The riches and splendour of the Hoysala court were already evident in their grand temples at Belur and Dvarasamudra (present day, Halebid). The Hoysala temple at Somnathpur, is truly unique in design, perfect in proportion and the stone carvings are striking marvels in stone. The shrine stands in the centre of a walled compound, around which runs an open verandah with sixty four cells. The temple itself, stellar in shape, has three elaborately carved pinnacles with a common Navranga and stands on a raised platform. The three sanctums once housed beautifully carved idols of Kesava, Janardhana and Venugopala. Today the idol of Lord Kesava is missing, but the other two still adorn the sanctums in their original form. The friezes on its outer walls with their intricately carved rows of elephants, charging horsemen, and mythological birds and beasts leaves one spellbound. Beautifullysculpted images of gods, goddesses, and scenes from the epics, as well as the remarkably ornate ceilings in the pillared hall are very beautiful. At the temple, the outer walls are decorated with a series of star-shaped folds and the entire surface is covered with carved stone plaques. Shravanbelagola, is one of the most important Jain pilgrim centres of India. The statue of the Jain saint Gommateshwara (981 CE) is one of the tallest and most graceful statues in the world. It is carved out of a mountain and is situated in the Indragiri hills. The colossal monolithic statue is fifty eight feet high, with twenty six ft wide shoulders, ten feet of its feet. Starkingly simple, the beautifully chiseled features of this statue embody serenity. Nearly 1,800 years old, the statue which is reached by climbing seven hundred steps carved in the steep granite slope, is symbolic of the renunciation of worldly possessions. It was sculpted by Aristanemi in 981 CE and Chamunda Raya, a general and minister of the Ganga King Rachamatta installed it in 983 CE. Lord Gomatesheshwara was the Jain prince Bahubali. During a war with his greedy elder brother, Bharata who wanted to grab the kingdom, Bahubali accepted defeat at the moment of his victory when he realized the futility of it all. He renounced the world and left to lead a life of penance and meditation, attaining nirvana. Thousands of devotees congregate here to perform the Mahamastakabhisheka. It is a spectacular ceremony which is the focus for Jain pilgrims across India, held once in twelve years. Hundreds of pots containing curds, milk, honey, vermilion, coconut water, turmeric paste and even gold and precious jewels are poured over the statue's head by priests. In addition to the statue, there are several Jain temples and monasteries in Shravanabelagola and it attained historical importance when Chandragupta Maurya, the greatest King of Mauryan Empire, settled on this hill in third century BCE, along with his Guru Bhagwan Bhadra Bahu Swami, after renouncing his kingdom.

Yakshagaana is believed to have a history of one thousand years and is believed to represent a specific type of music of the yakhas. Yaksha are the demi-gods attending on 'Kubera'- the god of wealth in the Hindu mythology. Gaana means song. By combining the meaning, the term Yakshagaana might mean the 'song of Yakshas'. Of the twenty districts in Karnataka, Yakshagana has established its firm roots in the districts of Dakshina Kannada, Uttara Kannada, Dharwad, Mysore and Hassan. The epics of Ramayana and Mahabharata offer extensive material for Yakshagana prasangas (or themes). The literature is presented both in verse and prose and the former is interpreted in simple prose and dialogues. The show begins with an announcement of Yakshagana by beating the drum, in important places of the village. Yakshagana is performed in a rectangular stage built with four wooden poles installed on four corners and covered by mats of palm leaves on the top. Away from the backstage is a small place called 'chowki', the greenroom for the artistes. The audience sits on all the three sides of the platform and a curtain covers only the back stage. In the Yakshagana , the Bhagavata is the chief narrator of the story, who recites it in verse form. Bhagavata also conducts light hearted conversation with the Vidushaka- the jester. The dialogues between these two characters is very amusing and the Bhagavata ably supports the Vidushaka in carrying out extempore dialogues. Music is the essence of Yakshagana and the narration is in verse form. It is the songs and poems which transmit the story and the songs are invariably sung by the Bhagavata. The music is excellent and synchronizes well with the costume and make up of the characters. Prose in Yakshagana is in the form of dialogues. The songs sung by the Bhagavata are at a very high pitch and hence is considered as a distinct style of music. The rhythm that dictates the body movements, footwork and the performance actually flows from the musical instruments.

Chennapatna is well known for its unusual wooden lacquered toys and products. These craftsmen called chitragars are involved in this traditional craft since ages and make beautiful toys like a grinding stone, mortar, pestle and rolling pin, as well as a well to hold water. Other creations include Wood turning requires extremely close grained and moderately hard wood and Hale wood is the most suited wood found in this region. The required size and shape of wood is cut, seasoned, attached on to a lathe and turned in order to smoothen it. Chisels are used to shape the revolving piece of wood and flaws are sandpapered away with. Karnataka has a huge forest-belt and sandalwood carvers are found in Bangalore, Mysore, Shimoga, Honavar and Kumta on the coast. Sandalwood is of great religious importance and is an extremely expensive material for carving artifacts. Sandalwood is of two types: srigandha which is close grained and yellowish-brown in colour and used for carving; and nagagandha which is darkish-brown in colour and from which oil is extracted. Sandalwood is a rich, golden brown wood that gives off a fragrance. The wood is cultured and used to make a plethora of products that range from idols of deities and finely twisted chariots to decorative pieces such as paper cutters, walking sticks, trays, boxes and elephant figures. Jali or fret work with patterns in high and low relief are generally seen on them.

Description: Mysore and Bangalore are the main centers for rosewood carving and artists make beautiful decoration and utility objects from this. There are temples and palaces which have ancestral art of wood carving on the bracketed pillars, door frames and arches. Rosewood furniture and elephants fitures are the products which are always in high demand. Wood inlay is the process of decorating the surface of wood by setting in pieces of material such as ivory, bone, plastic, or wood of different colours. This craft is also concentrated in Mysore and Bangalore where its roots can be traced back to a family by the name of Mirza Yusuf Ali who was pioneer in the field. The artisan smoothens the base of the rosewood and the design is traced and etched into the surface. The several components of the inlay are painstakingly assembled to match and fit exactly into the grooves and are then glued in. The design is finished by obtaining the required shades with several coats of polish. Examples of some famous inlay work in Karnataka include the ivory inlay in rosewood and ebony in the Srirangapatnam mausoleum; the doors of the Amba Vilas palace in Mysore are also fine examples of inlay. Products with inlay include plates, boxes, bowls, cigarette cases, and figures of animals, especially elephants, which continue to be popular. The designs include floral and geometric patterns, landscapes, pastoral scenes, processions, and scenes from the epics.

The carvings depict the deepalakshmis or women holding lamps. The sanctum known as srikovil is double storeyed and square in shape. The mandapa is made of stone which again depicts the Tamilnadu style of architecture.

The Paradesi Synagogue The grand and glorious synagogue known as Pardesi synagogue named after the foreigners who were the Jews from Spain and Portugal. This is one of the oldest synagogues built in the sixteenth century, being the only one in use even today out of the seven built in the Jew town. It was the king of Cochin, Paraja, who gave a piece of land to the Jewish community next to his palace to build the synagogue. It was reconstructed in 1662, after the Portuguese bombardment. Outside the synagogue, there are wrought-iron gates decorated with the Star of David. The rectangular building is white-walled and tile-roofed, with an inner courtyard lined with ancient Hebrew-inscribed grave stones. There is a Dutch-style square clock tower with four clocks featuring four different numerals: numerals facing the synagogue. Roman numerals, Malayalam numerals,and Arabic numerals facing the rest of thethree sides towards the public . At the bottom of the tower there is a well and inside the tower hangs the pendulum. The floor is paved with hundreds of old hand-painted porcelain tiles brought from China and no two of which are identical. The synagogue has a rich collection of gold and silver decorated Torah-scrolls crowned with solid gold and set with gems given as gifts by the kings, an oriental carpet and two brass columns symbolizing the pillars of the temple. In addition to this there is a collection of 10 paintings depicting the history of the Jews in the area.

The Mattancherry Palace is also known as the Dutch palace. It was built by the Portuguese in 1557 and presented to Raja Veera Kerala Varma of Kochi. The palace was renovated in 1663 by the Dutch and it took on its present popular name Dutch palace after 1663, when the Dutch carried out some extensions and renovations in the palace. The palace has two floors and a central courtyard which is in the traditional Kerala style of architecture known as nalukettus. The palace has a European character from the outside with scraped masonry walls and round-headed windows and doors but its sloping tiled roof and wooden balconies are local in features. The two arches at the entrance are typically Portuguese in character. Inside the inner court, there stands a small temple dedicated to Bhagavati, the protective goddess of the Kochi royal family. Two more temples are situated on either side of the Palace dedicated to Lord Krishna and Lord Siva. The interiors of the palace arepanelled with wood and has exhibits of the kings of Kochi like ceremonial robes, headdresses, weapons, palanquins, furniture but the main feature is the series of astonishing murals, depicting scenes from the Ramayana, the Mahabharata, and the Puranic legends connected with Shiva, Vishnu, Krishna, Kumara, and Durga painted on the walls as well as the portraits of the kings. The paintings cover a wide range of themes from the Puthra Kameshti Yagyam to Rama's return to Ayodhya after vanquishing Ravana. The paintings totally cover nearly 1000 sq.ft in area and date from as early as the 16th century through mid nineteenth century and are found in the chambers on the west side of the palace, in four chambers upstairs, and in two low ceiling rooms that are entered by a steep stairway. These beautiful and extensive paintings are fine examples of Kerala mural paintings best known for its unique style. The king's room is covered in about 48 paintings illustrating the Ramayana, from the beginning of the sacrifice of Dasaratha to Sita's return from captivity in Lanka. These paintings are the earliest in the palace, dating as early as 16th century. The last five scenes are from the Krishna Lila. Another important series of paintings in the Dutch palace is found in the upper rooms, notably that of the coronation hall that was made under Dutch patronage. Among the compositions are Lakshmi seated on the lotus, sleeping Vishnu (Ananthasayanamurti), Ardhanariswara and other goddesses, the coronation of Rama, Krishna lifting Mount Govardhana etc. The ladies chambers depict scenes from Kumarasambhavam and other works of the great Sanskrit poet Kalidasa. The dining hall has carved wooden ornate ceiling decorated with a series of brass cups. The palace also contains rare examples of traditional Kerala flooring, which looks like polished black marble but is actually a mixture of burned coconut shells, charcoal, lime, plant juices and egg whites.

Onam is a time for sports, festivities, and ritual celebrations in Kerala. This festival is celebrated in memory of the golden era of King Mahabali whose spirit is said to visit the state at the time of Onam. Colorful water festivals are organized along the sacred river Pampa as part of the celebrations. The festival is held at the end of August or beginning of September depending local calendar. The celebrations last for ten days and the last day is called the Thiruonam which is the most important day of celebrations. People make a preparation of a floral carpet called Athappookkalam in front of houses, from the first day of Atham to the tenth day of Thiruvonam. All over the state celebrations, rituals, where everyone participae wearing new clothes, prepareing traditional cuisine, and dance, and music mark this harvest festival. Aranmulla is the place for the exciting snake boat races. Nearly 30 chundan vallams or snake boats participate in the festival with fishermen singing traditional boat songs as they move their boats.
Thrissur Pooram Festival

The Napier museum is one of the earliest museum in India established by the Maharaja of Travancore in 1855. It is a ninteenth century structure, built in the Indo-Saracenic style and is a magnificent piece of architecture and is named after the former Governor General of Madras, Sir John Napier. Also called the Government Art Museum, this beautiful museum has an ornate interior and exterior. The building was designed by an English architect. The Sree Chitra Art Gallery inside the Napier museum features a rare collection of paintings by Raja Ravi Varma, Roerich and some works from the Rajput, Mughal and Tanjore schools of painting. Another attraction at the museum is the oriental collection comprising of paintings from Japan, China, Bali and Tibet. The museum has a vast collection of sculptures in bronze and stone, carvings of wood and ivory, lamps, textiles, Kathakali models, handicraft items, traditional musical instruments, a treasure of coin collections representing Chera, Chola, Pandya dynasties of Southern India. The bronze sculptures include fascinating images of Siva, Vishnu, Parvathi and Lakshmi. The Vishnu image of eight century collected from Ambalapuzha temple in central Travancore Pallava style is one of the oldest metal image from this region. The stone sculptures belong to eight to eighteenth century. All the wood carvings exhibited here shows high degree of excellence.

The Ambalavayal Heritage Museum, the archaeological museum in Wayanad, has one of Kerala's largest collections of the bits and pieces of an era dating back to the second CE. The displayed pieces here support the fact that an advanced civilisation existed in the mountains of Wayanad. The articles on display are a fascination for historians, archaeologists and common men alike. The museum boasts of articles as varied as clay sculptures, ancient hunting equipments like bows and arrows, stone weapons and other curios.

The Archaeological Museum set in a majestic building is an architectural delight. It houses a gallery of murals from all over Kerala and preserves a rare treasure of Veerakallu, temple models, olagrandhangal (manuscripts on dry palm leaves), megaliths etc. Veerakallu translated as herostones are stone engravings and sculptures of figures and weapons belonging to the heroes of days gone by which were recovered from the forests of Wayanad and Thrissur. The megalith collection includes earthen pots, urns etc. The temple models cast in plaster of Paris are excellent representations of the ancient temples of Kerala.

Description: Bamboo mat painting is one of the major handicrafts industries of Kerala. The local artists are skilled in this traditional art. Their work is first initiated by placing the correct size of mat which is utilized as a canvas for the painting. Then the basic coating is done on the mat which is then followed by the design on it. In these bamboo mat paintings the craftsmen depicts religious images, images of the birds and animals, human images as well as capture beauty of nature. These are highlighted with bright colours. The artists design all these paintings in different sizes which gives a very colorful look that is beautifully presented in appealing bamboo reed frames.

Kerala is famous for its diverse martial arts such as. Kalaripayattu, Parisa Kali, Velakanni. Kalaripayattu is the oldest existing martial art form in the world which dates back more than 2000 years. It is believed to be the forerunner of popularly known Chinese martial arts, originally from India, theBuddhist monk Bodhidharma took this knowledge from India to China. Said to have originated from the Dhanur Vedic texts, the practice of Kalaripayattu encompasses all fighting arts and is described by the Vishnu Purana as one of the eighteen traditional branches of knowledge. Kalaris are the schools where training in this martial art form is imparted by masters. Kalaripayattu requires a unique harmony of mind and body along with energy, flexibility of the body and sharp focus of the mind. Kalaripayattu involves increasing the flexibility of the body. The student learns to twist, jump and flex his/her arms that will help when learning the next stage. The second stage involves learning how to handle wooden sticks and other wooden weapons. The third stage involves handling metal weapons. The final stage involves fighting with bare hands. The students are taught arm locks, wrestling and defense. The Parisa Kali of north Malabar and Velakanni of Travancore are two other martial arts forms of Kerala, which involve considerable physical training and knowledge of the use of arms. Velakanni represents the battle between Pandavas and Kauravas at Kurukshetra, and is played during the temple festival at Cherthala.

Kathakali is the most popular dance Kathakali drama form of Kerala. The word Kathakali literally means story-play and it is known for its elaborate makeup and exquisite costumes have become the most acknowledged symbols for Kerala. The themes of Kathakali are religious and mythological and generally deal with the Mahabarata, the Ramayana and Puranas. Kathakali is usually performed by men and female characters are also portrayed by men dressed in women's costume. However, in recent years, women have also started becoming Kathakali dancers. Kathakalis tradition dates back to the seventheen century. It was given its present form by Mahakavi Vallathol Narayan Menon, who was the founder of the Kerala Kala Mandalam. The actors rely very heavily on hand gesture or mudra and eye movements to convey the story. Usually the large and heavy costumers of Kathakali are of different kinds meant for each character such as the hero, heroine or the villain who are instantly recognisable by their characteristic makeup and costume. The elaborate makeup, using different colors is more like a mask than makeup in the usual sense. The white is made fromrice flour, the red is made from vermilion (a red earth such as cinnabar). The black is made from soot. The colors are not merely decoration, but symbolize the characters. For instance, red on the feet is used to represent evil characters and evil meanings.

Name/Title: Kerala- Performing Art- Dance- Mohini Attam
Description: Mohini Attam is a dance form of Kerala performed only by women. The typical costume for Mohini Attam is generally simple white, or off-white saree with a golden Zari or red border, worn in a typical style. One of the most characteristic signs of the Mohini Attam dancer is the bun of hair worn off-centre. The dance is based on the myth of Mohini. The story is about how Vishnu decides to foil the demons in their plans to steal the churned out of ocean. He takes the form of a beautiful apsara, and by way of her amorous charms distracts the demons from stealing the amrit or the celestial ambrosia that gives immortality and power. The dance is slow, and extremely lyrical in style.

Name/Title: Coconut shell, Fibre and Stem Craft
Description: Coconut trees grow all over Kerala, and all pasts of the tree are use for making various prodence. Products like bowls, vases, tea pots and hookahs are crafted from coconut shell. Lamp stands encased in brass and smaller coconut shell articles are also made in Trivandrum, Attingal and Neyyatinkara, while larger items are made in Quilandy in Kozhikode district in north Kerala. Often hookahs and large vases are also made by combining coconut shells with brass bindings. Coconut fibre is cleaned, smoothened and made into various dolls and toys with beads and coloured threads to give it a decorative appearance.

Aranmula, a small village in Kerala is renowned for making special type of metallic mirrors with bell metal, an alloy of copper and tin. It is believed that a divine visitation inspired a widow of this village to discover a mysterious blend of bronze which could be waxed bright into crystal clear mirror. These mirrors are known as Aranmula Kannadi. This is the only mirror of its type, which reflects from the front. It is believed that owning such a mirror is a lifetime possession which brings good luck and brings prosperity and keeps evil eyes away. A technique similar to lost wax method is used to make moulds of these mirrors with the local mud from the field. Once the casting is done, the surface is polished with oil and some metallic powder. The polish may continue for several days to get the required surface. Kannans, the artisans of this unique type of bell-metal are only a handful of familes in the area, who retain till date, this art of getting such reflection from metal.

 A practice of Kerala, it is considered one of the oldest forms of martial arts worldwide. Legend says that it originates from Parashurama, the great sage, who is deemed to have been the creator of Kerala. Recent researches connect it to the Sangam Period, 600–300 BCE. Developed as a self-defence mechanism, the training is based on the scientific marma knowledge of Ayurveda and has movement phrases which are based on animal stances and movements.

Kathakali is a traditional dance from Kerala, primarily performed by men. It is like a colourful play, where dancers act out stories from Indian epics
using stylised facial expressions, hand gestures and body movements. There are two styles the northern style known as vadakkan and the southern style known as thekkan. The basic stance in kathakali is atimandala —a deep, grounded posture with knees bent outward and feet placed on the side-foot firmly planted apart. The dancers wear bright costumes, big crowns, and heavy makeup. Their faces are painted in colours that match their characters, like green for heroes, red for villains, etc. Every part of the face is used to convey emotion, while the dance is full of powerful poses and eye movements.

Ladakh has many historic monasteries called Gompas, where Buddhist Bhikkus (Bhikshus) and Bhikshunies have been living, studying and practicing their religion. Located in scenic locations the monasteries of Ladakh are, on hills and mountains and have rich collections of Buddhist Thangka paintings, art and artifacts. Alchi, a village in the Leh district is famous for one of the oldest monasteries in Ladakh, mainly known for its wall paintings of the eleventh century reflecting artistic and spiritual details of both Buddhism and Hindu kings of that time in Kashmir. The monastery was built by Lotsawa Rinchen Zangpo. At Alchi there are three shrines; the main one called Dukhang or Assembly Hall,the three-storeyed Sumtseg, and the Manjushri. There are also the votive stupas called the great Chörten and the small Chörten. Dukhang is the oldest monument preserved at Alchi. The entrance to the temple is through a courtyard and an elaborately carved doorway with panels of tiny Bodhisattvas and guardian figures. The hall has a niche at the back with a plaster image of Vairocana. The hall is painted with different mandalas. The entrance is flanked by an only partly preserved Life of the Buddha and a large depiction dedicated to donors and their the sides of the Alchi Photo Gallery niche is a depiction of attendant figures, feasts. Below the thousand Buddhas painted on animals and sacred symbols. Sumtseg, is dedicated to a triad of Bodhisattvas and their secondary deities located in three niches. The facade is carved in wood consisting of pillars, carved brackets, and capitals. Light penetrates through open shafts on each floor. The largest Bodhisattva on the back wall, Maitreya, is flanked by Avalokiteshvara and Manjushri. Besides these each niche has four secondary deities and two flying goddesses .Each of the Bodhisattvas are dressed in beautifully decorated garments. The Manjushri Temple is square with a large central platform. It supports the four pillars holding the diagonally arranged cross-beams of the ceiling. The four images of Manjushri are seated back to back in an elaborate common frame crowded various images of animals, gods and symbols and topped by the decorative scrolls deriving from the tails of the makaras. The Hemis Gompa is the biggest monastery in Ladakh.

One of the finest examples of architecture from Ladakh, Thicksey Monastery is one of the most important monasteries. It houses one of the largest Buddhist statues, the 15 meter tall Champa, the Buddha of Future. About a hundred monks live here who follow traditional ways of running the monastery and teach monks and villagers. This Gompa is situated on the top of the hill and the 12-storey monastery complex contains numerous stupas, statues, thangkas, wall paintings, swords and a large pillar

Known as the temple city of India, Khajuraho is known for its intricately carved, beautiful medieval temples. A symbol of India's glorious past, heritage and culture, the temples symbolize an immortal saga of Hindu art and culture in central India and are an outstanding image of the well developed Nagara style of temple architecture. Khajuraho was the historic capital of the Chandelas who built these temples from the ninth through the thirteenth centuries. Among the 85 original ones only 25 have survived the ravages of time. Around the temples are bands of fine work, portraying gods, goddesses, musicians, animals, etc. Erotic sculptures featuring apsaras and mithunas (couples) also dominate the themes portrayed here. shrine and four subsidiary shrines scattered around the landscape. The temples of Khajuraho are divided into three groups- the western,which is the largest group having temples dedicated to Shiva and Vishnu like Chitragupta Temple, Kandariya Mahadeo, Chausat Yogini Temple, Lakshmana Temple and Matangeswara Temple. The Eastern are the Jain temples including the temples of Pashvanath and the Adinatha which were built by the merchants and the Southern group, where the remains of the Vaidyanath Shiva temple has been exposed by the ASI (Archaeological survey of India). Khajuraho shows a highly evolved stage of Indian temple architecture. Most temples stand on a tall platform known as the Jagati. The elevation consists of three divisions: a pitha, the wall or jangha, and a roof or shikhara. Ornamentation is abundant on the basal storey in a series of mouldings. It depicts human activities, kirtimukhas and geometric designs. The wall section is divided into two or three sculptural sections including apsaras, mithunas and divine figures. As these figures rise upwards they add to the dramatic effect. The oldest of these temples, dating back to 900 CE is the Chaunsath Yogini temple, located southwest of the Shibsagar lake. Built of rough granite it is dedicated to the sixty four manifestations of the Mother Goddesses or the yoginis. This shrine is raised on a large platform in an open courtyard surrounded by miniature shrines for sixty four manifestations of the goddess. Kandariya Mahadeo temple is the largest in Khajuraho. It is considered to be the best representation of the nagara style of temples consisting of a garbhagriha or a sanctum, a circumambulatory path - pradakshinapatha, an antarala or the vestibule, ardhamandapa, mandapa and a mahamandapa. The sanctum enshrines a marble shivalingam. This mammoth structure stands 30 metres above the ground level. A rich variety of sculptures adorn the platform. They are sculptures of female figures in different poses engaged in writing letters, playing with a ball or applying makeup. The northern group has Vaishnava temples for the most part and the south eastern group consists of Jain temples. To the north of this temple is the Devi Jagadambi temple standing on the same platform as Kandariya Mahadeo. It is more delicately proportionate and the temple is decorated with some fine sculptures. Due to its smaller size, the sculptures are clearly visible. Further north is the sun temple, enshrining an image of the Sun God, on a chariot pulled by seven horses. To the extreme north of this, is the Vishwanath temple, built along the lines of the Kandariya Mahadeo temple. Inscriptions reveal that it was built by King Dhanga and that an emerald image of Shiva - Marakateswara was enshrined here. South west of this temple is the Parvati temple. The Lakshmana-Chaturbhuja temple stands on a platform which has a magnificent sculptural frieze of elephants and horse riders in a procession. There is also an embellishment of erotic sculptures. The Matangeswara temple enshrines Shiva, in the form of a highly polished gigantic Shivalingam. There is also a small Varaha temple with a gigantic monolithic image of a standing Varaha, the boar incarnation of Vishnu. The whole figure is carved in low relief. The main sanctum contains the image of Vaikunth Vishnu, bearing three heads representing his various incarnations. The eastern group has temples dedicated to Brahma. It is one of the smallest shrine with a single room having a shiv- linga protected by a huge pyramidal roof. Vamana and Javari are miniature versions of the western group of temples.

Name/Title: Adinath Temple, Parsvanath Temple, Ghantai Temple, Hanuman Temple and Brahma Temple
Description: Among the temples in the eastern zone, the ones worth mentioning are: Adinath Temple, Parsvanath Temple, Ghantai Temple, Hanuman Temple and Brahma Temple, which can be divided into two, the temples dedicated to the Jain pantheon and the temples dedicated to Hindu Gods and Goddesses. The Jain temples include the Parsavanath Temple dedicated to Parsavanath, the Jain Tirthankara. It is a well decorated and the largest Jain Temple. Adinath temple is dedicated to Adinath, a Jain Tirthankara. The sculpted figures of Yakshis are particularly famous here. Ghantai Temple is well known for the sculpture of a Jain goddess on a winged Garuda and for the sixteen dreams of Mahavira's mother. The temples in the southern zone has Dulah Deo temple dedicated to Lord Shiva and Chattarbhuj temple. The Dulah Deo Temple has been dedicated to Lord Shiva. It is supposed to have been constructed between 1100 CE and 1150. Inside the temple there is a vast Shivalingam. There is also an image of Lord Shiva at the very entrance of the temple.The architectural complex consists of the mandapa, where the shrine is placed, along with the mahamandapa and the ardhamandapa with no circumbulatory passage. There is also the cluster of the shikharas, both subsidiary and centralized. The Chaturbhuja temple consists of the shrine of Lord Vishnu, to whom this is dedicated. This temple has also been constructed in the 1100. The structure is more or less similar to the Dulah Dao Temple. The exotic sculptures add to the glamour and elegance of the place.

Ram Raja Mandir, a palace-turned-temple has a charming legend attached to it. King Madhukar Shah brought an idol of Lord Rama from Ayodhya to his capital following the dream visitation of God Ram to be installed later in a temple. When the idol proved impossible to move, the king recalled, too late, the deity's edict that the image would remain in the place where it was first installed. It is also the only temple in India where Ram is worshipped as a king. Chaturbhuj Temple was built upon a massive stone platform and reached by a steep flight of steps. The temple was specially constructed to enshrine the image of Ram which, however, remained in the Ram Raja Temple. Lotus emblems and symbols of religious importance provide the delicate exterior ornamentation. Laxminarayan Temple A flagstone path links the Laxminarayan Temple with the Ram Raja Temple. The style here is a mix of fort and temple architecture. The interiors contain the most exquisite of Orchha's wall paintings. On the walls and ceilings of three halls, these murals are vibrant compositions and cover a variety of spiritual and secular subjects.

The Chanderi fort is located in the small historical town of Chanderi in the Ashoknagar District of Madhya Pradesh. The fort is the most striking monument in this ancient town and it dates back to the Mughal Period. The Muslim rulers, especially the Malwa Sultans took a lot of initiative to construct the fortification walls of the fort. The mahals within the fort were built by the Bundela rajputs revealing various phases of building styles. Located on top of a hill, the fortified walls enclose the citadel and protect it from outsiders. The Fort is approached through three gates. The first and main gate is well known as the Khooni Darwaza. It has been so named because criminals were thrown from the battlements above and their bodies crashed to pieces below. Hawa Paur is the third and highest gate of the Chanderi fort. The remnants of the Chanderi Fort include the Hawa Mahal and the Nau Khanda Mahal. Both these buildings were built by the Bundela chiefs. There is yetanother gateway on the south western side of the fort referred to as the Khatti Ghatti which is about twenty five metres in height forming part of the outer defenses of the town. There is a Purana Madarsa which was used as a school in the sixteenth century. It has latticed screens with geometric designs set in closed arches and the walls are embellished with lotus medallions. There is a massive structure known as the Koshak Mahal which houses four identical palace buildings which are situated at the corner of a square courtyard. The plain exterior contrasts well with the ornate bay windows. The battisi baoli is the biggest step-well in Chanderi. Thirty-two broad steps from each side descend down to a square pool.

Lal Baag palace is located in Indore. It is surrounded by gardens and was built between 1886 and 1921. It is one of the grandest ancestral monuments built by the Holkar dynasty. The rooms have been restored and furnished and much of the furniture and ornamentation is in the early Georgian style. Its Italian marble columns, grand chandeliers, rich Persian carpets, flying nymphs on the ceiling, Belgian stained glass windows, Greek mythological reliefs, Italian style wall paintings speak of its past glory.

As the name suggests, the full temple is made up of coloured glass. This Jain Temple was built by the Cotton King Sir Hukamchand in the early twentieth century. Inside this Jain temple thousands of mirrors adorn the walls, floor and ceilings, supplemented by brightly patterned ceramic tiles, Chinese lantern-type glass lamps and cut glass chandeliers. The use of glass beads and raised figures produces a pleasing three-dimentional effect. The paintings done in coloured glass depict stories from Jain scriptures.

The Rajawada with its 7-storeyed gateway is a mixture of French, Mughal and Maratha styles. Its lofty entrance archway above a huge wooden door encrusted with iron studs, leads into a vast courtyard enclosed by galleried rooms. The lower three floors are made of stone and the upper floors are made of wood.

Mandu was built by the Paramara ruler Raja Bhoja and was once the capital of Malwa. It was built in the fifteenth century as a summer retreat. Jahaz Mahal is a unique monument in the shape of a ship which connects two lakes Kapur Talao and Munj Talao. Its unique construction shows the taste and the prosperous art and architecture of the past. Jahaz Mahal was built in fifteenth century when the place was under the rule of Ghiyas-ud-Din. Hindola Mahal means a swinging hall. It was built under the rule of Ghiyas-ud-din. The monument is an audience hall which is adorned with wonderful sculptures. The mahal was built with sand stone with beautifully carved columns. To the western front of the mahal there are few other mahals whose identities are not yet unveiled. Champa Baoli is a construction that stands in the midst of the Mahal depicting the past. There is a provision of hot and cold water that are also connected with the underground rooms.

Gwalior is an ancient city which was under the illustrious rule of the Scindias prior to India's independence. Gwalior was once known as Gopadri or Gopachala. It has relics from the period of the Guptas, Huns, Pratiharas, Tomaras, Pathans, Moghuls, Marathas and the British. Among the temples of interest at Gwalior are the Chaturbhuj temple, the Sas Bahu temple and the Teli Ka Mandir. The Chaturbhuj temple dedicated to Vishnu is located on the eastern road to the fort. It is a rock cut monolithic structure and it was built in the year 875 during the rule of the Pratiharas. The Sas Bahu temples are located on the eastern slope of the Gopadri hill. Both of these temples, built in the Nagara style of architecture are dedicated to Padmanabha or Vishnu. Ornately decorated, the doorways, ceilings, and the

Sanchi, one of the most distinct archaeological sites in India is located right in the middle of the country. The world heritage site of Sanchi is being represented by various monuments including stupas, monolithic Asokan pillar, temples, monasteries and great sculptural wealth built over several centuries from the early Mauryan period to the twelfth century. It was Emperor Asoka who laid the foundations of a religious centre at Sanchi by erecting a monolithic pillar. He erected the stupa 1 here after redistribution of mortal remains of Lord Buddha for erecting several stupas all over the country in order to spread Buddhism. This stupa was originally a low structure of bricks, half the diameter of the present edifice hemispherical in shape with raised terraces at the base. It was enclosed by a wooden railing and a stone umbrella at the top. This great stupa later served as a nucleus to the large Buddhist establishment. Ashoka built a total of eight stupas on the hilltop of Sanchi including the great stupa. A number of stupas and other religious structures were added over the succeeding centuries. With the decline of Buddhism, the site decayed and was eventually completely forgotten. But, between1912 and 1919, the structures were rediscovered and carefully restored to their present condition. Originally stupas were mounds covering the relics of the Buddha or his followers. In its earliest stages Buddhist art didn't represent the Buddha directly. Instead, his presence was alluded to through symbols such as the bodhi tree, the wheel of law or his footprint. The stupa also became a symbol of the Buddha. More exactly, it became a symbol of his final release from the cycle of birth and rebirth - the Mahaparinirvana. During the Sunga period, several edifices were raised at Sanchi and its surrounding hills. The Ashoka stupa was enlarged and faced with stones and decorated with balustrades, staircases and a harmika on the top. In the Ist century BCE the Andhra-Satavahanas, whose boundaries covered the Malwa region, added the elaborately carved gateways to stupa 1 which is the most elaborate and well known of more than fifty magnificent Buddhist monuments that crown the hilltop of Sanchi. A nearly perfect hemispherical dome, the great stupa1 is topped by a triple parasol set within a square railing or harmika. A third of the way up from its base, a raised terrace, enclosed by a fence, is meant for ritual circumambulation of the monument. A second, stone-paved procession-path at ground-level is enclosed by an encircling stone balustrade. This path is accessed from the cardinal directions through four exquisitely carved gateways. The exquisite carvings of the doorway depict in detail the significant episodes and miracles from Lord Buddhas life and events depicted in the Buddhist jataka stories. The eastern gateway depicts the young prince, Gautama leaving his father's palace on his journey towards enlightenment and the dream his mother had before his birth. The western gateway depicts the seven incarnations of the Buddha. The northern gateway crowned by a wheel-of-law, this depicts the miracles associated with the Buddha as told in the Jatakas. The southern gateway shows the birth of Gautama revealed in a series of dramatically rich carvings. From the second to fourth century CE Sanchi and Vidisha came under the rule of Kushanas and Kshatrapas and subsequently passed on to the hands of the Guptas. During the Gupta period some temples were also built and sculptures were added displaying the classical grace and simplicity of the era. Further, statues of Lord Buddha seated in the canopies facing the four entrances of the great Stupa were also added. Sanchi also flourished during the seventh century when shrines and monasteries were continued to be added. Thus Sanchi displays harmonious co-existence of Hindu and Buddhist faiths.
