The city of Orchha was founded on the banks of Betwa in the sixteenth century by the Bundela chief Rudra Pratap, who became the first ruler of Orchha. In the early seventeenth century, Raja Jujhar Singh rebelled against the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, whose armies devastated the state and occupied Orchha from 1635 to 1641. The main historical monuments of Orchha are the Jehangir Mahal, Raj Mahal, Rai Praveen Mahal, Laxmi Narayan Temple and the Chaturbhuj Temple. The various palaces and temples built by the Bundela rulers retain much of their immaculate perfection. Of the succeeding rulers, the most notable was Raja Bir Singh who built the exquisite Jehangir Mahal, a tiered palace crowned with graceful Chhatries. Construction of the Raj Mahal was started by Rudra Pratap, and completed by one of his successors, Madhukar Shah. The Sheesh Mahal was built during the early 18th century, and was originally intended as an exclusive country retreat for the local king Udait Singh. It has two rectangular courtyards inside, the second, formerly used by the Bundela queens. Opulent royal quarters, raised balconies and interlocking walkways rise in symmetrical tiers on all four sides, crowned by domed pavilions and turrets. One can find the fragments of mirror-inlay and vibrant painting plastered over their walls and ceilings. Some of the friezes are still in remarkable condition. The Rai Praveen Mahal is a small, double-storeyed brick apartment built by Raja Indramani for his concubine in the mid seventeenth century. This building lies to the north of the Sheesh Mahal. The building, set amid the lawns of the Anand Mahal gardens, it has a main assembly hall on the ground floor, a private salon upstairs, and cool underground apartments. Entered through an ornate ceremonial gateway, the east-facing facade is covered with turquoise tiles. Two stone elephants flank the stairway, holding bells in their trunks to announce the arrival of the Raja. Three storeys of elegant hanging balconies, terraces, apartments and onion domes are piled around a central courtyard. This palace, however, is more airy and lighted since it has countless windows and pierced stone screens looking out over the skyline to the west, and a sea of treetops and ruined temples in the other direction.

Name/Title: Fresco is a technique where the painting is done when the plaster on the wall is still wet therefore the colors intermingle permanently with the plaster and is permanent.
Description: Mural painting refers to paintings on walls, ceilings, or other large permanent surfaces. This style of painting can be traced back to prehistoric times such as the paintings on the Caves of Lascaux in southern France. The term Mural came into being with the Mexican muralista art movement. Fresco is a technique where the painting is done when the plaster on the wall is still wet therefore the colors intermingle permanently with the plaster and is permanent. For quite some time the art work was mistakenly referred to as "frescoes". We now know that the proper term for this kind of artwork is known as mural because the known process and technique of fresco painting isn't found in this kind of art. At Ajanta, the technique and process used to produce this kind of artwork is unlike any other artwork found in the art history of other civilizations. These murals have a uniqueness about them. The process of painting involved several stages. The first step was to chisel the rock surface, to make it rough enough to hold the plaster. The plaster was made of clay, hay, cowdung and lime. Differences are found in the ingredients and their proportions from cave to cave. While the plaster was still wet, the drawings were done and the colors applied. The wet plaster had the capacity to soak the color so that the color became a part of the surface and would not peel off or decay easily. The colors were referred to as 'earth colors' or 'vegetable colors.' Various kinds of stones, minerals, and plants were used in combinations to prepare different colors. Sculptures were often covered with stucco to give them a fine finish and lustrous polish. The stucco had the ingredients of lime and powdered sea-shell or conch. The latter afforded exceptional shine and smoothness. In cave upper six, some of it is extant. The smoothness resembles the surface of glass. The paint brushes used to create the artwork were made from animal hair and twigs.

Balaghat has a lovely green stone out of which the local carvers make a number of small items, animals, boxes, trays, etc. But the important products are the religious images.

Madhya Pradesh is well known for papier-mâché items. The main center for papier-mâché is Ujjain but this craft is also popular in Gwalior, Ratlam and Bhopal. Craftsmen from Gwalior and Bhopal make statues of birds, animals and decorative panels. The craftsmen of Ujjain make papier-mâché birds and figures of popular deities. These products

The tradition of making a special type of traditional rag dolls is prevalent in Gwalior.The faces of these dolls are painted beautifully and the eyes are painted in such a manner that they give them a very lively expression. The dolls are dressed in paper costumes in traditional style. The dolls are highly decorated and ornamented. These dolls are popularly known as battubai dolls as they were created by a woman named Battubai.

The Maheshwari saree in Madhya Pradesh has an unusual origin for it is traced to a generous queen who once ruled over that territory and designed the first saree. Maheshwar, the place itself is a charming one on the banks of the river Narmada. The Maheshwari saree, mostly in cotton is characterised by its simplicity . The body is either plain or has stripes or checks with several variations. A speciality of the Maheshwari saree is its reversible border because of which either side of the saree can be worn. This is locally known as bugdi. The borders have a wide range of mat designs which consists of floral designs, the best known amongst which is the karanphool pattern.

Madhya Pradesh has very unusual and attractive bandhanis or tie and dye work. The best known centres are two villages in western Madhya Pradesh on the opposite banks of river Gujari known as Tarapur and Umedpura. Mandsaur also produces some excellent bandhani. Amongst the wide selection of designs the most common is of chains of grains represented by dots on the body called the dana pattern while there are elaborate designs on the borders and pallus.

The Malwa region of Madhya Pradesh has long being known for its printed cotton textiles which are printed in different techniques like direct dyeing and printing, resist dyeing and printing, rogan printing and screen printing. The important centres are Jawad, Bhairongarh, Tarapur, Umedpura and Sheopur. The communities engaged in this craft are chippa, rangrez and nilgar. Jawad was once famous for exporting the reknowned jazams to various countries under royal patronage.

The durries of Madhya Pradesh, from Jobat and Tipgaon in the tribal district of Jhabua are well known for their sturdy character and delightful colours. Weaving in Jobat is simple, done on the pitlooms with panja, a woodden apparatus, almost like an extension of the hand, used to pull back firmly and fix the weft yarn in place. These mats are very attractive because of their delightful warm tints.

Kathak, which means storytelling, is a dance form from northern India, particularly rooted in the regions of Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan. Kathak evolved as a form of storytelling through expressive gestures, intricate footwork and graceful movements. Dancers captivate audiences with swift  spins, rhythmic foot stamping, delicate hand gestures, and nuanced facial expressions to bring stories to life. Among the many gharanas of kathak the Lucknow, Jaipur, Banaras, Raigarh styles are particularly renowned though several other gharanas have also shaped and enriched the form. They stand tall in a posture called sama sthana, with feet together or in a slight v-shape. The costumes are usually long, flowing dresses like anarkalis or lehengas, with dupattas made from fabrics typical to northern India.

Name/Title: Aurangabad- Monument- Kailasanatha Temple at Ellora
Description: A marvel of engineering and artistry Kailasanatha temple dates back to the period of the eight century Rashtrakuta period. It is a collosal monolithic rock cut temple built in the Dravidian style and is known for its architectural grandeur as well as its sculptural splendour. More than thirty temples have been carved from the hillside at Ellora during the period sixth to ninth centuries CE. Its excavation must rank as an architectural wonder. Two great trenches some ninety meters long were dug into the hillside. They were connected at the deepest point by another trench fifty three metres across. The temple was meant to appear as though rising from a vast courtyard at ground level. The great block of residual rock, rising thirty metres, was then carved into the three- storeyed vimana, the main mandapa, two giant dhwajasthambas or pillars, and four sub- shrines. Beginning at the top, the mass of rock was hewn into shape, and as each layer was shaped, the carvers began ornamenting the structure moving downward, thus eliminating the need for any scaffolding. The temple is dedicated to Shiva and named after his abode in the Himalayas, the Kailasa. It was built during the period 757 and 773 CE. The temple covers a large area and the vimana (tower) rises to a height of about ninety feet. The most amazing thing to be emphasized over and over again and seen to be believed is that the entire monument was made by excavation and not by construction. The typical Dravidian features includes a gateway, an enclosure for the Nandi, and a mandapa lined up in front of the sanctum which is crowned with a vimana, composed of successively receding storeys, decroated with miniature buildings. The mandapa in front of the sanctum is an enormous pillared hall with elaborate carving. On either side of the Nandi mandapa are two fifty feet high obelisk like pillars decorated with frieze carvings. Two storeys of corridors have been carved into the mountain, ringing the temple on three sides. These corridors are studded with small alcoves, all containing a wealth of sculpted figures telling the tales of the great Hindu epics, the Mahabharata and the Ramayana. Among the narrative friezes is the descent of river Ganga, and one of Ravana shaking Mount Kailasa. The architectural style and intricate sculpture is similar to Virupaksha Temple at Pattadakal that had been completed a decade before. A collonaded gallery running along the bottom of the cliff face forms a deep narrow passage that surrounds the temple. In between this cliff face and the temple is the pradakshinapatha. The temple tower resembles the rathas at Mamallapuram near Chennai in Tamilnadu. The Kailasanatha temple resembles the architectural style established by the Pallavas of Mamallapuram and is yet considerably grander in scale. Other caves of interest in Ellora are the Rameshwar cave, the Sita ki Nahani cave, and several Jain caves such as the Indra Sabha cave, all dating back to the period of sixth-ninth centuries CE.

Name/Title: Mumbai- Monument- Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus (formerly Victoria Terminus)
Description: The Chhatrapati Shivaji terminus, formerly known as Victoria Terminus in Mumbai was designed by Frederick William Stevens. It is an outstanding example of Victorian Gothic architecture in India, blended with themes deriving from Indian traditional architecture. The terminal was built over ten years starting in 1878 according to a design based on late medieval Italian models. Its remarkable stone dome, turrets, pointed arches, and interesting ground plan are close to traditional Indian palace architecture. The interiors are adorned with wood carving, tiles, ornamental iron and brass railings, grills for the ticket offices, and the grand staircase with balustrades.

The Gateway of India, a massive archway on the Apollo Bunder, is one of the grand and magnificent landmarks of Mumbai, which was built to commemorate the visit of the British Monarch, King George V and Queen Mary. The Gateway of India is one of the hot spots of Mumbai city. Designed by the architect George Wittet it was formally opened in 1924 by the then Viceroy, Earl of Reading. The Gateway is a 26m high structure with four turrets and complicated lattice work engraved into the yellow basalt stone. The central dome of the Gateway of India is 48 feet in diameter. It is interesting to note that the whole harbour front was realligned in order to come in line with a planned walkway, sweeping down to the centre of the town. At the back of the Gateway arch, steps lead down to the sea front.

The Elephanta Island is located ten km away from the Gateway of India at Mumbai. These caves house rock cut temples dating back to the fifth century CE. Elephanta Island was so named by the Portuguese, after the statue of an elephant near the landing area of the island. There are six caves dating back to sixth and seventh century. These rock cut temples dedicated to Lord Shiva are abundant in sculptural content. Created by carving out rocks, and creating columns, internal spaces and the images, the entire temple can be compared to a huge sculpture. Some of the rock surfaces are highly finished while some are untreated bare rock. The entire cave temple consists of a main chamber and two lateral ones, courtyards and several subsidiary shrines. Above the temple is the mass of natural rock. There are three entrances to this temple with the one on the east and the west marking the axis of the temple. A twenty pillared hall lines the axis, and on its western end is the cella in which is enshrined a Shiva linga. The pillars consist of fluted columns standing on square bases, and are crowned with fluted cushioned capitals. The most enigmatic image is of Trimurti or the Sadasiva manifestation of Shiva which is a collossal twenty feet high image of the three headed Shiva. Also on the southern wall are grand sculptured images of Kalyanasundara, Gangadhara, Ardhanariswara and Uma Maheswara. To the west of the northern entrance are sculptured images of Nataraja and Andhakaasuravadha urth, and to its east are images of Yogiswara and Ravanaanugrahamurthy in eight manifest forms. At Elephanta caves, Shiva is portrayed in the non-anthropomorphic Shivalinga form, as well as in the colossal human image. The secondary shrine is located to the east of the main temple in a courtyard. This temple contains six pillars at its entrance, four of which are free standing and two connected. The entrance leads to a hall decorated with sculptured panels depicting legends from the Shiva Purana.

Bibi Ka Maqbara, the burial place of Aurangzeb's 1st wife, Rabia-ud-Durrani is an imitation of the Taj at Agra and is often referred to as the poor mans Taj Mahal due to its poor copy of the masterpiece. The mausoleum is made mostly of sandstone and has plastered walls and a marble dome.The tomb is adornedwith lattice work in marble and inlay decorations of flowers and creepers which are beautiful. A high wall with bastions runs around the monument and the recesses have little minarets. The entrance leads to an arch and from this point, a fine view of the structure ahead may be obtained. The pavement that leads to the mausoleum is flanked by oblong reservoirs.

Once known as Devagiri, this place was later renamed as Daulatabad by the then Sultan of Delhi, Mohammed - bin - Tughlak. One of the world's best preserved forts of medieval times the fort has hundreds of secret passages. The fortress was built to be secure with three massive walls to defend it against enemy attacks. The fort has some impressive structures like the Chand Minar, Jami Masjid and Royal Palace which are worth mentioning. The palace also has a few spacious halls, courtyards and pavilions.

Kanheri caves were the viharas for the Buddhist monks during the period between second century BCE and ninth century CE. These caves are simple and bare, quite different from that of Elephanta caves which are artistically embellished. Kanheri caves are mostly tiny cells that are cut into the edges of a hill, each having a stone plinth that might have served as a bed. There is also a congregation hall supported by huge stone pillars that contains the dagoba, a kind of Buddhist shrine. The largest is the Cave 13 which is adorned with sculptures in front of the stupa.

The Bhaja caves near Lonavla are the perfect examples of the phase of early Buddhist architecture. Lord Buddha has been represented here through numerous symbols in the caves. However, the caves which were carved after the fourth century CE, also presents the Buddha in his physical forms. The pillars of these caves are carved with figures of flowers and other images. The cave 12, is a Chaitya hall, which is the largest of all has a fine vault. The last cave towards the south is a good example of fine architecture and sculpture. This cave includes the figures of a dancing couple, a prince seated on an elephant and The remaining 7 caves contain inscriptions about the donors. The chaitya caves do not have a wall in the front as they are open which might have been enclosed by a wooden door of some kind in olden days. The patterns of the ceilings are prototypes of wooden ceilings.

The Buddhist caves at Karle, built by the Buddhist monks, are the epitome of ancient rock-cut caves to be found in India. Dating back from the second to first century BCE, the Karle caves in Lonavla, were built during the Satvahahana period and hosted the monks in the monsoons, Built from top to bottom in the form of a ladder, the early Karle caves do not depict the Buddha in his physical forms but rather in symbols. However, from the seventh century CE when the Mahayana became more popular with their liberal thoughts, the later Karle caves do present the Buddha in his physical form such as the Buddha preaching while seated on a lion-supported throne, along withother magnificent carvings. The caves comprise mainly two types of structures: chaitya halls and viharas. The chaitya halls, which form the largest number of chaityas in the world (one being one hundred and forty eight feet long), were used for congregational worship whereas the viharas were the dwelling place for the monks and further included cells cut into the walls around three sides of a hall used for their residential and individual meditation. The pillars of the halls inside the caves have been carved with figures of men, women, flowers and elephants, though the pillars outside these halls have lions erected on them as their crowns, an emblem of Ashoka, the great Indian ruler.

Name/Title: Maharashtra- Fairs and Festivals - Ganesh Chaturthi
Description: Also known as Vinayak Chaturthi, Ganesh Chaturthi is a festival celebrating the day on which Lord Ganesh, son of Shiva and Parvati appeared on earth for his devotees. According to the Hindu calendar, Ganesh Chaturthi is celebrated on the Shukla Chaturthi which is usually between 20 August and 15 September. The festival lasts for almost 10 days. The festival commences with the installation of the idol of Ganesh in beautifully decorated pandals. The pandals are decorated with paintings depicting the life of Lord Ganesha. The festival also includes a lot of cultural activities like music and dance. A popular sweet made during the Ganesh Chaturthi are modak and karanjis which are sweets made of coconut, jaggery, and other flavors.

Name/Title: Maharashtra- Fairs and Festivals- Parsi New Year
Description: The Parsi New Year is also known as Navroze and is mainly celebrated by a particular sect of Parsis, the Faslis. It is also celebrated by the Muslims of Iran and Zoroastrians. Navroze is the first day of the first month according to the Zoroastrian calendar. Originally an agricultural festival, the Parsi New Year later transformed into a religious festival. The day is celebrated by wearing new and colorful clothes, decorating the house with colours, lighting incense sticks and sprinkling sandalwood powder on live coal. The day begins by going to the Fire Temple and offering Jashan or a thanksgiving prayer service and offering sandalwood to the holy fire. Food is a significant part of the Parsi New Year. It includes a wide selection of non-vegetarian dishes, fruits and nuts. Two important dishes in breakfast for the Parsi New Year are Ravo and fried vermicelli cooked in sugar syrup and decorated with raisins.

Name/Title: Mumbai- Museum- Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Vastu Sangrahalaya (Prince of Wales Museum)
Description: Some prominent citizens of Bombay decided to set up a Museum with the help of the government to commemorate the Prince of Wales, the Crown Prince who visited Bombay in 1905 and later became King George V, who laid the foundation stone of the museum. The exquisite basalt stone structure with its large central dome inspired by the Bijapur domes and beautiful gardens are set in a crescent shaped piece of land. Art, archaeology and natural history are three exclusive sections in the museum. It houses some of the finest collections, ranging from ancient Indus Valley relics to the artifacts from the Gupta and Maurya Periods. Here, one can see a few of the rarest and earliest exhibits of Indian history. There are scores of interesting artifacts from foreign countries like Tibet and Nepal. It has one complete gallery comprising the exquisite thangka scrolls of the Buddhists. Another gallery is devoted to bronze castings and stone sculptures and more than 2,000 miniature paintings from the different styles and phases of India. The collection presents the evolution of painting in India, ranging between eleventh and twelveth century illustrated palm leaf manuscripts to early nineteenth century Pahari paintings. Exquisite examples of all the main schools of miniature painting are on view, Rajput, Mughal, Pahari, and Deccani, each school with its characteristic style has its own delicacy of form and colour. The variety of art displayed in the museum is definitely a treat for any art-lover.

Dr. Dinkar Kelkar started collecting artifacts and objects around 1920s and by the sixties he had accumulated around 15000 exhibits. He was a great lover of Indian art. The Kelkar Museum is the result of his tireless efforts of about sixty years. It is a museum with a collection of everyday objects like pots, lamps, containers, nutcrackers, pen stands etc. Objects have been classified according to their materials and techniques of making them and their function. There are some unique collections in this museum. There is an assortment of oil lamps made of different materials right from clay to brass, each with their own shape and form and usage right from rituals, to practical lighting.Some beautiful, intricately carved wooden doors and windows adorn the museum. They are collected from Gujarat, Rajasthan, Karnataka and Kerala. Another kind of collection is of locks used for both trunks and doors. They are of interesting shapes of dogs, horses and even scorpions. One remarkable collection is the chitakathi scroll paintings which tell us the great tradition of the village storyteller and accompaniment of music and song.

Description: Warli painting derives its name from a tribe living in the remote regions of Maharashtra. Their imagination, beliefs and customs are freely and spontaneously expressed in their monochromatic paintings. The walls of the village of Warli have been adorned with these paintings for centuries and even today they form the primary decoration in most of the houses. Their way of life, trees, birds, men and women form composite paintings, and the most joyous celebration of their life. The moods of their life make for interesting themes, which is why Warli paintings are much more than designs on walls; they are authentic depictions of a way of life. The Warlis live in thatched mud-huts, which are constructed in such a way so that they all surround a central common area. They are primarily an agriculture-dependant tribe. Historians believe that the Warli tradition can be traced back to the neolithic period between 2500 BCE and 3000 BCE. During the harvest season, and weddings and births, their houses are adorned with a variety of patterns. The Warli way of life is beautifully captured in simple images in white against earthen background. Geometric designs dominate most paintings; dots and crooked lines are the units of these compositions. Spiral formations of men and women and concentric circular designs are symbolic of these paintings. The harmony and balance depicted in these paintings is supposed to signify the harmony and balance of the universe. Marriage is the most common theme of Warli paintings. Many paintings have a depiction of Palghat, the marriage God, accompanied by a horse and of course the bride and the groom. These paintings are sacred and without them the marriage cannot take place. Men and women in spirals dancing in celebration, is another theme typical to the Warli paintings. A musician playing a native instrument is usually found in the middle of such spirals. Flora and fauna are also depicted in these paintings.

Tamasha is a form of theatre, which came into existence in the early sixteenth century in Maharashtra, which includes the love songs i.e. lavanis due to which, this folk art, was very popular among the common people. Lavani is a combination of traditional song and dance, performed by women. It is performed to the beats of dholak. The word lavani originates from lavanya, meaning beauty. Earlier, this art form dealt with different and varied subject matters such as society, religion, politics, romance, etc. It is said that Lavani was used as a form of entertainment and morale booster to the tired soldiers during the eighteenth and nineteenth century Maratha battle. Many famous Marathi poets like Honaji Bala, Ramjoshi, Prabhakar, have written for Lavani.

Koli is one of the most popular folk dance forms of Maharashtra that derives its name from the fisher folk known as Kolis. It is a dance of joy, which is a celebration of valuable life, performed with sheer exuberance by the dancers. Both men and women in groups perform these dances, where all the performers have to make a single row or stand in pairs and portray many fishing actions in the dance form, by holding small oars in their hands and moving those to the beats of the songs. Generally, women participants wear green coloured sarees in their Koli style, whose length comes upto their knees; while the men wear a lungi having a triangular shape. The dance sequences include actions like rowing of a boat, or movement of waves, where swaying of oars in backward and forward direction creates a scene of a boat tossing on the high sea-waves. Ellora is the finest example of cave temples with almost thirty four caves with intricate interiors and ornamental facades. Carved during the 350 CE and 700 CE, the rock temples and monasteries represent three faiths - Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism. Cave 10, a Chaitya-hall is popularly known as Visvakarma' with a seated Buddha in a stupa. The Ramesvara cave has figurines of river goddesses adorning its entrance. The Dumar Lena cave is dedicated to Lord Shiva. Among the viharas, Cave 5 is the largest. The most impressive vihara is the three - storeyed cave called 'Tin - Tala'. The Kailasa temple in cave 16 is a masterpiece in itself. The temple that took nearly hundred years to be completed is decorated with themes and incidents from the puranas. Consisting of exquisite carvings, the cave temple is the most striking one amongst the other 30 at the site. Though carved out of one single rock, the temple looks like a freestanding structural southern type temple. The exterior of the temple is richly carved with niches, plasters, windows as well as images of deities, mithunas (erotic male and female figures) and other figures. Most of the deities at the left of the entrance are Shaivaite (followers of Lord Shiva) while on the right hand side the deities are Vaishnavites (followers of Lord Vishnu). The whole temple consists of a shrine with a ling at the rear of the hall with a Dravidian shikhara, a flat-roofed mandapa supported by sixteen pillars, a separate porch for Nandi surrounded by an open-court entered through a low gopuram. There are two Dhvajastambhas Ajanta Photo Gallery (pillars with the flagstaff) in the courtyard. The grand sculpture of Ravana attempting to lift mount Kailasa, the abode of Lord Shiva, with his full might is a landmark in Indian art. All the carvings are done in more than one level. The lower storey consists of several large shrines while the gallery along the three sides at the rear contains huge sculpted panels. A two-storeyed gateway on the west side provides access to the main temple and the Nandi mandapa, both on the same level, and is approximately seven meters high. The lower storey of the main temple as well as the Nandi shrine is solid but unaccessible. Stone bridges carved from the living rock connect the Nandi pavilion and the entrance porch of the temple. The main temple has a southern style superstructure. The lower storey has almost life-size elephants carved as if they are holding up the temple. The Jaina Caves (30 to 34) are massive, well-proportioned, decorated and mark the last phase of the activity at Ellora.

Kohlapuri chappals are handcrafted leather sandals that get their name from the place of their origin, the district of Kohlapur. Intricate patterns are handcrafted and made of leather; the interesting fact is that even the cords used to stitch the sandals are made of leather and no nails are used. The hide of bulls, cows, and goats are used for the leather. Kachkadi, bakkalnali, and pukari are some traditional designs. Kohlapuri chappals range from those with simple straps and plain colours and designs to more decorative ones with a gold cord or gota on them. These chappals, which were probably worn only by the inhabitants of Kohlapur, are now worn all over India and abroad.

Savantvadi in Ratnagiri district is famous for its unique, brightly coloured lacquered toys and dolls, imitation fruits and vegetables. The best known is a set with a man and a woman and a toy winnowing fan in folk style. They mainly show men and women in either standing or sitting postures. Hale and pangora wood is used by the traditional craftsmen who are known as chittorees (picture makers). At one time this was a big craft centre for the round lacquered highly pictorial playing cards known as ganjifa.

A very beautiful style of saree called paithani named after the village Paithan is a well known handicraft of Maharashtra. On a zari wrap thread the weft is interlocked with different colours. In this technique, complicated patterns of flowers and birds are woven in bright colours. Asavali (vine and flowers), Narli (coconut design) and petal design are the few traditional motifs. Due to the closeness of Paithan to the famous Ajanta caves, there are motifs of Buddha woven standing or in the sitting posture and motifs of gold coins are also represented in the weaves. The pallu is an exquisite piece of gold tissue around which are woven brightly coloured rosettes and birds.

Ganeshpur in Bhandara district is famous for tusser silk weaving. It is the main occupation of the Koshti community which is half the working population of this district. They claim to be descendents of sage Makaranda known to have woven the first fabric from lotus fibre to clothe the gods. Tusser silk produced here is known by its Sanskrit name kosa. Some varieties of tusser silk produced in this area are motha choukada - a design in big squares, lahan choukada - a design in small squares, gunja salai - diagonal designs on cloth along with coloured lines at regular intervals in green, blue or orange, teen dhari choukada -- the three square pattern, and rasta choukada -- square pattern with horizontal lines running through.

Aurangabad is famous for Mashru and Himru fabrics. These two types of fabrics are made of cotton and silk having a shine like satin. The ornamental design is formed on the principle of extra weft figuring. The extra silk weft left loose makes the Himru shawl soft, which almost feels like silk. Weavers were brought to Aurangabad from Banaras and Ahmedabad by Mohamed-bin-Tughlak and thus the Himru industry started.

Bamboo, is abundantly grown in Churachandpur, Jiribam, Tamenglong and Imphal districts of Manipur. Manipur is the largest producer of bamboo products after Tripura in the entire north-east region. Some of the bamboo products are sofa sets, mats, basketry, tray, chair, table, flower vase, ashtray and other decorative and utility articles.

Stone carving is a traditional craft of Manipur. In Bishnupur district utility items like bowls, candle-stands, grinders, flower-vases, stone glasses, plates, etc. are made. In Manipur there is a custom of constructing an engraved memorial stone for their deceased describing their achievements and good deeds on the outskirts of the village. So making stone carving was popular even from earlier days.

Imphal valley of Manipur is the centre for kauna crafts. This is often used for making mats, chairs, cushion, coasters, bags, moorah (low stools) etc. A unique craft of Manipur is the double-weave mat known as the kaunaphak reed mat. Known as phak in Meithei, a language of Manipur, the reed used to weave the mat is called kauna. The mat is made by the local people for their own use, as well as for commercial purposes. Phak is yellow in colour and is the succulent stem of a plant that grows in water. Reeds are carefully chosen for the mats. The plant is cut only when it has reached maturity. Once cut, the stems are dried and become soft and quite brittle. A bunch of cut stems of the appropriate length are then woven with bamboo placed at suitable distance to give the mat its desired length. The border has an interesting pattern and is about an inch wide. The kauna reed mats are not meant to be washed as the reed gets spoilt with moisture.

Textile weaving is a house hold industry in Manipur. Coarse cotton cloth and silk is woven on the looms. Cotton thread is imported in large quantities. Cotton yarn is dyed with red, yellow, green, orange, black and pink colours. Artistic designs are arranged horizontally and vertically by producing stripes and geometrical blocks. These blocks are filled up with geometrical designs of smaller components. The rhythm of colour bands is maintained. This craft is also known by the name of Laichamphi which means cotton cloth. However, loin loom weaving caters to the local demands and requirements only.

In Manipur dolls and toys are made from different materials like cloth, cotton, clay, wood and bamboo etc. They have a charm of their own with their traditional outfits. Dolls include characters like Radha Krishna, and toys include stylized animals and birds forms.

Performed at festivals combining dance & drumming. The Pung, or Manipuri drum is the soul of Manipuri dance. The Pung Cholom dance is performed during the festival of Holi. The Pung Cholom or Drum Dance is a visual interpretation of the various rhythmic patterns played on the pung. In this dance, the drummer identifies completely with the intricate rhythms he plays on the drum and expresses it through corresponding body movements and footwork. The Pung Cholom is part of the music of the Sankirtan tradition and is acclaimed as one of the best art forms of the state. 

In the Pung Cholom dance of Manipur, the drummers jump and spin holding a drum. (Ref: NCERT Textbook gekr1, Ch. 11)

Manipuri is a classical dance from Manipur in NorthEast India. This dance form is soft, gentle and flowing. The movements are smooth and round, almost like gliding. The dancers always look calm and peaceful. The dance includes raas leela (stories of Krishna) and traditional movements from Lai Haraoba. Manipuri dance also includes Sankirtan, a devotional music and dance form performed with cymbals and drums, often as part of temple rituals. The famous costume is the poloi dress—a stiff, colourful skirt with a veil and elegant jewellery. The men wear white dhotis and turbans, especially during pung cholom or raas performances.

The festivals of Mizoram are related to the agricultural activities that bring forth the vibrancy and the liveliness of the people of Mizoram. Some of the major festivals in Mizoram which can be mentioned are Chapchar Kut, Mim Kut, Pawl Kut and Thalfavang Kut.

Name/Title: Mizoram- Fairs and Festivals- Chapchar Kut
Description: Chapchar Kut, the spring festival is the most important in Mizoram. People of all ages, men and women, dress themselves in traditional and colourful costumes and wear exotic headgears and jewellery. They assemble and perform various folk dances and also sing traditional songs accompanied by beating of drums, gongs and cymbals. The groups from every region come to the event and display their best performance. The performers dance in joyous celebration of life. Cheraw or the bamboo dance which is popular all over the country is also performed during this festival. The Mizo dances are associated with their respective festival celebrations. More popular dances like the Cheraw are performed almost in every festival of the state.

On Christmas Eve, the people start celebration in their homes and on Christmas, a grand celebration takes place in the church. Next day the people have a grand and sumptuous feast where everyone from young to old take part and rejoice with great fervour and festivities.

Name/Title: Mizoram- Handicrafts - Cane and Bamboo Work
Description: The Mizos expertise in wicker-work and basketry is well known. Even their houses are generally built with bamboo walls and floors and thatched roofs. While women excel at weaving, men are expert at cane and bamboo work. They make fine cane hats and uncommonly beautiful baskets. The traditional Mizo hat is known for its workmanship. The fine woven bamboo hat looks as fine as cotton yarn. A typical Mizo basket is broad at the rim and tapers at the bottom. There are baskets for carrying firewood, water, paddy, rice and vegetables. Baskets made of cane and bamboo together with leaves and grasses, for storing ornaments, clothes and other valuables are also made. Bamboo is also used in traditional ornaments. while celebrations, Mizo women use a headgear of a bamboo band with parrot feathers stuck in it, the ends of which are decorated with beetles. Other bamboo products include fish and animal traps, rain bamboo hat seen with the formation of a flat thin layer on its top, japis, cones, circular boxes and other materials serving as reservoirs and containers of goods, crops and other things. Both Mizo men and women love their locally made pipes. The womens pipe is like a small hukkah, small enough to be easily held in the hand and carried about. The mens pipe is of western type. These are made out of bamboo and weed.

Basketry among the Mizo is a delicate work. They are experts in making etches and notches from the soft fibres of cane. Baskets with lids and without lids, smoothly surfaced, strongly floored, gently fenced from mouth to base and modelled into oval, square, flat structures, revealing a considerable skill in slitting, folding and inserting are seen. They serve various purposes such as cages, containers, baskets of different articles, etc. Some forms of baskets made in Mizoram are dawrawn, empai, emping, tlamen, paikawng, hnam, paiem, fawng, thul, etc.

The cane baskets of the Khonoma village and of the Khiamngan weavers in the Tuensang District are known for their intricate weaves. Fine bamboo and cane strips are also used for making headgear and mats. These baskets are well known for their utility as well as for aesthetic value.

Spinning and weaving is an exclusive monopoly of the women. Colourful shawls, bags and jackets are woven here. The natural dyes used by them are extracted from barks, roots and plants. Works of each tribe can be identified by the distinguishing colors and motifs which are often based on folklore.

Woodcarving is another work of artistry by which Naga people are known. It can be explained under three heads namely headhunting, decoration of the Morungs, and funerary images. Though most of the tribes have skills in woodcarving, the Wanchos, Konyaks and Phom tribes are the finest wood-carvers in this genre.

The pots are generally very simple and mainly functional. Some of the designs and the motifs found on these potteries have been inspired by the design of the textiles. The pots of villages of Tseminyu and Ungma are well known in the region. These pots are made on the pottery wheel, then the pot is heated and finally rice water is boiled to remove the taste of the baked clay and ensure durability.

Some of the crafted items are spears, chisels, ornaments and items of utility. Nagas are attached to their weapons and it might be because their survival in the past depended on this skill. These weapons are different in shape and pattern from tribe to tribe. Among all the tribes, the Rengmas are considered the best blacksmiths.

Name/Title: War Dances -  Angami, Ao, Sumi tribes – Warrior tradition, Konyak, Lotha, Chakhesang dances
Description:
Sumi war dance - The Ao Naga tribe from the northeastern part of Nagaland celebrates the Moatsu Mong festival as a time of recreation and joy, after the hard work of clearing fields, burning jungles, and sowing seeds. It is marked by vibrant songs, dances and merrymaking. Another major festival, Tsungrem Mong, is observed on the eve of the harvest to offer gratitude to the Supreme Power, with colourful costumes, songs and dances. The Ao Naga have a rich tradition of clothing that distinguishes between commoners and warriors, with the Ao warrior known as mangkotepsu. The Sumi tribe performs the energetic Sumi war dance to celebrate victory in battle, while the Lotha women perform the mungyanta, a harvest dance during the Tokhu Emone festival. Nagaland is home to around 30 traditional dances, including the Sangtam War Dance, Hornbill Dance, Chang Lo and Butterfly Dance, each reflecting the cultural richness of its many indigenous communities.
One of the important persons who has contributed a lot to the dances of the community is Sangyusang Pongen of the Ao community. He received the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award for his contribution. (Ref: NCERT Textbook hekr1, Ch. 11)

The largest and most outstanding example of Nagara style of temple building at Bhubaneswar, the capital of Orissa and a city of temples is the Lingaraja Temple. Also Bhubaneswar has been referred to in several of ancient texts as a sacred pilgrimage center. Dedicated to Lord Shiva, Lingraja temple is almost a thousand year old. The Lingam here is a unique Hari Hara lingam  representation of half Shiva and half Vishnu. Located in a spacious courtyard and fortified walls, the temple has an elaborately carved vimana or tower which rises up to 180 feet and has several vertical sections, the recesses of which are filled with more miniature vimanas.The temple consists of a Nata Mandir, Bhog Mandapa and a Jagamohan. The spacious courtyard is full of shrines, big and small, built in different periods and their number exceeding a hundred, of which only a few are of outstanding merit. The complex is enclosed by a massive compound-wall having an imposing gateway on the east and two secondary gates on the north and south. There are more than 150 other shrines around the main temple. The Shivalinga in the sanctum is 8 inches above the floor level, and is 8 feet in diameter. The Bhagawati temple is located in the northwest corner of the courtyard. There are several other shrines and temples in this vast courtyard. The largest structure known as the Sri Mandir is studded with 65 temples of different sizes. Once a year, an image of Lingaraja is taken to the Jalamandir in the center of the Bindu Sagar lake in Bhubaneswar.

The Rajarani Temple was built between the tenth and eleventh century from reddish gold sandstone known as Rajarani in the local language. It is a graceful and elegant structure which boasts of intricately carved figurines performing everyday activities. The temple stands on a raised platform and its spire is decorated with clusters of turrets (replication of the spire itself) emerging form the rib of the spire. The jagmohana is extremely plain, and was repaired in 1903 after having fallen down in ruins. The deul, on the other hand, is spectacularly ornate, and is famous for the aesthetic concept of miniature temple spires clustered around the main tower. The sculptural images of the temple are elegant and lively, especially the beautiful female figures which are in amorous, as well as engaged in such activities as holding children, looking in mirrors, and playing with pet birds. On the lower register of the deul, on the corner projection, are found the famous 'Guardians of the Eight Directions'. From the gateway in a clockwise direction around the porch and the deul to end back at the torana the eight guardians are Indra (god of rain), Agni (god of fire), Yama (god of death), Nirriti (god of suffering), Varuna (god of ocean), Vayu (god of wind), Kubera (god of wealth) and Ishana (Shiva).This Temple is the only one of its kind in the region of Orissa to have a cluster of small sized towers, or shikharas, in tiers which together make the main tower. Both the jagamohana and the deul are richly decorated.

Mukteswara temple is dedicated to Lord Shiva - Mukteswara and is carved with figures of ascetics in various postures of meditation. The relationship with older structures can be seen in the small size of the temple - 35 feet high. The latticed windows of the Jagmohana and the octagonal compound wall seems to have been patterned on an earlier structure, a torana (arched gateway), which was found in a field near Bhubaneswar during excavations. It is now in the Orissa State Museum. The extraordinarily beautiful sculptures include elaborate scrolls, graceful female figures, monkeys, peacocks, and a wealth of delicate carvings. Humorous and lively scenes depicting popular stories from the Panchatantra are carved around the windows of the Jagmohana. The image of a mythical lion head (shardul) with open jaws, flanked by attendants, over an elaborate horseshoe shaped chaitya is found on the southern exterior projecting wall of the tower and is a common feature of many later temples of Orissa. This is one of the first and the finest appearance of this image. There are a number of depictions of skeletal ascetics among the sculptural images, most of them shown in teaching or meditation. On the outer face of the compound wall are niches containing a variety of divinities. These include Saraswati (sitting on a lotus with two female attendants), Ganesa (with his attendant mouse), and Lakulisha (the fifth century founder of the Pashupata sect of tantric Shaivism), who is portrayed sitting cross-legged, with two miniature ascetic figures in the triangular side panels. Several small shrines with Lingam can be noticed within the compound.

Dhauli has major edicts of Ashoka engraved on a mass of rock. The edicts are remarkable and they have been excellently preserved, despite the fact that they date back to the 3rd century BC. The top of the rock is sculpted into an imposing elephant's head, which is the Buddha's mothers dream of the Buddha descending to her womb in the form of an elephant. The forepart of the elephant, hewn here out of solid rock represents the earliest sculpture tradition in Orissa. At Dhauli, Ashoka built several chaityas, stupas and pillars. This is said to be one of the earliest rock cut structure in India.

The rock art of Orissa dates back to as early as the prehistoric period, the earliest being the rock shelters of Vikramkhol dating to 1500 BC containing pre-historic, undeciphered pictographic inscriptions. The caves must have attracted people to live there, who decorated these rock shelters with paintings and engravings in various geometrical forms and figures of human and animal figurines. Drawn in monochromatic and polychromatic floral patterns they have withstood the test of time. The engravings still have traces of red ochre fillings.

Name/Title: Orissa- Monument- Cave Temples- Khandagiri and Udaygiri
Description: Khandagiri hills are known for fifteen rock cut caves while the Udaygiri hiils have eighteen caves. First among these is the Rani Gumpha. Used as a monastery it has corridors with a double row of pillars and a row of rectangular rooms. Above each entrance is an arch, resembling the torana reliefs. There are ruins of wooden temples on the hill. The Jain temple in Khandagiri belongs to the nineteenth century. In the caves around the temples, statues of various Tirthankaras sculpted between eleventh and fifteenth Century has been found.

Ratnagiri had been known as a centre for Buddhism during seventh to ninth century. It was also known for a university similar to Nalanda. On the peak of the hill, is the foundation of a stupa surrounded by a number of smaller stupas. There are also a small and a large monastery. The large monastery shows a dependence of the Gupta style of architecture, especially the Buddha carved around the entrance and on the doorway of the shrine. A number of Buddhist buildings were also excavated at Udaygiri. Statues from the Baumakara dynasty, a restored stupa with a chaumukha and a number of statues were also found there. A Buddhist monastery on the hill has a larger than life statue of Buddha enshrined in the central courtyard. There are beautiful sculptures on the pillars of the shrines entrance.

Konark is the abode of a magnificent temple dedicated to the Sun God. Built by King Narasimhadeva in the thirteenth century to mark his victory over the Mughal invaders, it is a colossal structure. Though in a ruined state, it is an outstanding example reflecting the genius of the architects who envisioned and built it. Referred to as the Black Pagoda the ruins of this temple were excavated in late nineteenth century with the tower over the Garbhagriha missing, although the jagmohana is intact. Devoted to the worship of Sun God it is built in the shape of a ratha carrying the Sun God drawn by seven horses. It is an excellent example of intricate sculptural work. The chariot of the sun god with 24 wheels, each about 10 feet in diameter, with a set of spokes and elaborate carvings has seven great horses who seem to strain to pull the weight of the structure. Two stone lions guard the entrance, crushing elephants. The jagmohana is 120 feet tall and is adorned with scenes drawn from the lives of the ordinary and the royal men. There are images of Gods and Goddesses, mythical creatures, dancers and musicians, women and men socializing at many levels that are carved of soft and weathered laterite and khodalite blocks. The nata mandir in front of the jagamohana is also intricately carved. Around the base of the temple, and up the walls and roof, are carvings in the erotic style in the manner seen at Khajuraho. There are images of animals, foliage, men, warriors on horses and other interesting patterns. There are three green chlorite images of the Sun God, positioned to catch the rays of the sun at dawn, noon and sunset. These figures are carved in very high quality and resemble bronzes because of their colouring and beautiful workmanship

Puri, on the east-coast of India, in the state of Orissa is a pilgrimage center, dedicated to the Lord Jagannath. Puri has an ancient temple, enshrining the wooden image of Krishna  in the form of Jagannath along with Balabhadra (Balarama) and Subhadra, brother and sister of Krishna on both the sides. Puri is located adjacent to the sea and the vast temple complex occupies an area of over 400000 square feet, and is bounded by a 20 feet high fortified wall. This complex contains about 120 temples and shrines. The shikhara of the Jagannath temple soars to a height of 192 feet. Structurally the temple has four chambers. The outermost is the Bhogmandir, the next is the Nata-mandir, or the pillared hall for music and dance, the next is the Jagamohana - or the mandapa where devotees gather for worship and the last is the sanctum or the Deul enshrining the deities. The temple was originally built by the Kalinga ruler Anantavarman Chodaganga and later on completed by King Ananga Bhima Deva Puri is one of the four dhams or peethas of God established by Sankaracharya, the other three being Sringeri in Kanchipura, Dwarka in Gujarat, and Badrinath in the Himalayas. Shri Chaitanya, the well known bhakti saint of the fifteenth - sixteenth century popularized the worship of Jagannath. The Rath Yatra or the Chariot festival in the month June  July is a spectacular chariot festival involving the procession of three massive chariots bearing the images of Jagannath, Balarama and Subhadra through the streets of Puri . Jagannath's chariot is a 35 square feet, rising to a height of 45 feet, with 16 wheels of 7 feet diameter each. More than 4000 people drag the chariot. Thousands of devotees gather from all over the country to witness this festival. New chariots are made each year.

Known as Rath yatra, this festival is celebrated in the honor of Lord Jagannath who is believed to be an incarnation of Lord Vishnu. The wooden images of Krishna, Balrama and Subhadraare taken out in procession in three chariots to their summer temple for a week. The ropes of the huge chariots are pulled by thousands of devotees. In the ancient times, devotees would occasionally throw themselves in front of the chariot of Sri Jagananath, for it was believed that to be crushed to death under its sixteen wheels was to go straight to heaven. Since Sri Jagannath is a form of Vishnu and Sri Krishna, many of the rituals observed in Puri temple are associated with events in the life of Sri Krishna. Thus this annual festival represents Sri Krishna's journey from Gokul to Mathura.

The art form essentially consists of inscribing letters and artistic designs on palm-leaf, mostly cut into standard sizes and held together with two wooden plank covers stringed through a hole in the center. Etching is done within lines using an iron pen on leaf strips. A paste made of bean leaves, charcoal made of burnt coconut shells, seasame oil and turmeric is rubbed on the etching that highlights the figures. Stories and incidents of Mahabharat, Ramayana and other epics are also etched. Scenes of nature are representated in paintings and drawings.

The Odissi dance is the classical dance of Orissa. It has a long, yet unbroken tradition that may be traced back to more than 2000 years. Dancers are found depicted in bas-reliefs in the hills of Udaygiri dating back to the first century BCE. The Natya Shastra speaks of the dance from this region and refers to it as Odra-Magadhi. Most notable people who popularised Odissi dance in the recent times are Guru Deba Prasad Das, Guru Pankaj Charan Das, Guru Raghu Dutta, and Guru Kelu Charan Mahapatra. There are a number of characteristics of the Odissi dance. The style may be seen as an accumulation of aesthetic and technical details. The Tribhangi is one of the most characteristic features of Odissi dance The concept of Tribhang divides the body into three parts, head, bust, and torso. Any posture which deals with these three elements is called tribhangi.

, guru and promoter of Odissi dance was born in Raghurajpur, a village near the temple town of Puri. He learnt to paint and sculpt at an early age and started playing in folk theatre groups at the age of nine. In 1994, he set up Srijan, an organisation dedicated to train students in Odissi dance. He was instrumental in projecting Odissi dance on the world stage in a big way in the early 70s and took this classical art form to a great level, His students include Sanjukta Panigrahi, Madhavi Mudgal, Protima Bedi and Sharon Lowen. Recipient of Padma Vibhushan, the second highest civilian award he died in Bhubaneshwar in April 2004. The themes of Odissi are almost exclusively religious in nature. They most commonly revolve around Krishna. The ashtapadis of Jayadevs Gita Govind are a very common theme. There are a number of musical instruments used to accompany the Odissi dance. One of the most important is the pakhawaj, also known as the madal. Other instruments which are commonly used are the bansuri (bamboo flute), the manjira (metal cymbals), the sitar and the tanpura. With numerous religions, ancient temples, local shrines, tribes and an array of sacred places, Orissa observes uncountable number of festivals and fairs round the year. Orissa has a large number of temples built in Nagara style of architecture, with distinctive features specific to this region. The three major temples Lingaraja temple at Bhubaneswar, Jagannath Temple at Puri and the Sun Temple at Konark represent the complete evolution of this style of temple architecture during the tenth century, was the peak of architectural activity. A temple in Orissa is known as a deul and it consists of a sanctorum, one or several front porches known as Jagamohana usually with pyramidal roofs, a dancing hall or the Nata Mandir and a hall of offerings called a Bhog Mandir.

Orissa is a treasure house of opulent artistic heritage. From specimens from the temple architecture, or be it the Applique artists of Pipli or the stone carvers of Orissa. The hereditary skill of artists has handed down the ages traditional arts and crafts like weaving of Ikat, Bomkai and Sambalpuri Sari. Stone carving, applique and embroidery are equally famous, silver filigree work, palm leaf incised design, metal work, lacquered craftsmanship all have acquired a unique place worldwide.

Ganjifa or the playing cards are made from circular pieces of paper on which intricate designs from the Dashavatar (the 10 Avatars of Lord Vishnu.) are hand-painted. There are ten sets of twelve cards each, housed in a colourful box. Each set is based on one of the ten incarnations of Lord Vishnu. They are painted on a canvas of three layers of gum pasted cloth and then coated with liquid chalk and polished with stone. Lacquer is applied at the back of the cards to give it stiffness. The black pigment used on the cards is obtained from soot by burning tin over a kerosene lamp. The best of ganjifa display fine lines and a pleasing delineation of features in the micro figures along with harmonised pleasing colours.

Pipli near Bhuvaneshwar is famous for its Applique craft. Fabrics of various colours are cut and stitched on a single colour base to form vibrant patterns. It was a craft practised for religious purposes especially for temples with embellished umbrella or fans of Lord Jagannath's as well as the auspicious temple tents. The applique work is done with great dexterity and the charming motifs include flowers, birds, animals at play and vignettes from every day life. The best of Orissa's applique work is noticeable due to the prominent usage of bold figures, flora and fauna and the use of vivid colours.

Orissa is a centre of pure silver Filigree work. Pure silver ingots are put through a wire drawing machine and the hair like wires are twisted and flattened. The thin wires are pleated and flattened again to get them as thin as the original wire and then bent into various shapes to form the required shape of the designs. The space within the frame is filled with creepers, flowers, etc. The effect is incredibly delicate, almost lace like. Orissa craftsmen make beautiful silver filigree jewellery, kumkum boxes, spoons, etc.

Orissa is famous for its ikat weave or bandha which has gloriously woven and blurred, coloured motifs in silk and cotton. The intricate process involves tie and dye - knotting sections of the yarn before dipping them in colours one at a time, and finally weaving them to produce motifs in multi-hued tones. The dominant motifs in this craft include animals and birds, with the traditional designs being fish and conch shell as well as bolmala, chandankora, and sachipar. While Sambalpur is famous for its double-ikat textiles, Sonepur is known for its gold embroidered ones.

Made on silk or on old cotton glued with paper, the Patachitra paintings are religious paintings which covers themes and events from Indian epics and Puranas. They exhibit the use of strong line and brilliant colors. Patachitras are painted in a regular series like Dashavatar of Vishnu and activities of Lord Rama and Krishna. These paintings have a basic resemblance to the old murals of Kalinga region dating back to fifth century BCE. The best Patachitra paintings are found in and around Puri, especially in the village of Raghurajpur. The artists colony, known as Chitrakar Sahi, is in the vicinity of the local temple. This art of painting on cloth can be traced back to the establishment of the shrine of Lord Jagannath at Puri in Orissa. Patachitra are made on cloth prepared with coating made from a mixture of chalk and gum. On this surface paintings are done with earth and stone colours. Apart from stories drawn from the epics popular patachitra themes are figures of Lord Jagannath, Balaram, Lord Krishna and events from His life. All this is executed in a riot of exuberant colours: dark green, lapis lazuli, parrot green, rose madder, bright oranges, yellows etc. The paintings are touched by a hint of gold and silver.

Soapstone and granite figures and icons are the special to Puri. Many of the figures are those of gods and goddesses, Apsaras and temple figurines. Different dance poses are beautifully executed on both granite and soapstone and brilliant craftsmenship and detailing go into the sculpting of jewellery on the figures, the fine depiction of stone trees laden with leaves, fruits, etc.

Wood carving, a major craft of Orissa includes painted wood carvings, plain wood carvings and teak furniture. The crowning glory of artistic woodwork in Orissa is its famous sacred trio - the images of Lord Jagannath (Krishna), Balabhadra (his brother) and their sister Subhadra which are made in Puri. Orissa is the storehouse for brightly painted masks carved out of wood, shola pith and other indigenous materials, for use in the sahi jatra, a professional form of theatre, which takes place at the time of Ramlila, but seems to particularly highlight the death of Ravana. Some of these masks are made in papier mache. The form is taken out on a mould but the actual face, specially the expression appropriately related to each character is carefully painted in pleasing combinations of colours.

Gotipua praises deities. The Gotipua Dance emerged from the ruins of the Devadasi tradition. From the 14th century onwards, political unrest and social changes took a toll on the Mahari or Devadasi tradition. During this time, attempts were made to keep alive the beautiful tradition of dance - thus was born the Gotipua tradition. The Gotipuas were young boys who were trained in singing, dancing and acrobatics in the village clubs or akhadas. They were dressed as girls and performed at temple festivals as well as various social and religious occasions. They also performed at special festive occasions relating to Radha and Krishna, like the Dol Utsav (or Spring Festival), the Chandan Yatra (or boat ride of Madan Mohan and Radhika on Chandan Pushkar) and the Jhulan Yatra (or Swing Festival). It is believed that the Gotipuas began their performance in the later medieval period, during the reign of the Bhoi King Ramachandradev. The present forms of Odissi dance have been derived to a great extent from the Gotipua tradition. Though the dances of the Gotipuas are in the Odissi style, crucial differences exist in technique, costume and presentation. Interestingly, the Gotipua dancers are the singers too.

Odissi, dance form originates from Odisha in eastern India. Various sculptural postures from the temples of Odisha are depicted in this dance form. The dance is smooth and flowing, with slow turns and graceful steps. This form has been derived from Maharis―Devadasis of Odisha and Gotipua ―group of boy dancers, dressed as girls who dance for Lord Vishnu. A special feature is the tribhanga pose, where the body bends in three places the head, torso, and hip.  Dancers often stand in a square-shaped and half-sitting pose called chauka. Costumes are made from traditional fabrics called pattasari (silk) with step fanshaped pleats and beautiful silver filigree jewellery and a flowerlike headpiece called tahiya.

Name/Title: Puducherry- Monument- The Church of Our Lady of the Angels
Description: The Church of Our Lady of the Angels was built in 1855, in a Greco-Roman architectural style. Its façade, has two plain square towers. The interior has a barrel vaulted roof, with a great dome rising over the crossing. The pastel peach and lime colours give the church a very serene appearance. This church is also famous for an oil painting of Our Lady of the Assumption, which was a gift from the French emperor, Napoleon III. The church has old pews (seats) made of cane, stained glass that filters sunlit patterns of colour into the interior.

Auroville - or the City of Dawn - was conceived as a place for human unity by the Mother, the spiritual collaborator of Sri Aurobindo. The idea is to build a futuristic city where people of goodwill can live together in peace and progressive harmony, above all creeds, all politics and all nationalities. Auroville came into existence in 1968. Located around eight kms north-west of Puducherry, Auroville was designed by the French architect Roger Anger. Around two thousand people live there in settlements with names like Grace, Fraternity, Fertile, Certitude and Transformation. The buildings are a combination of modern western and traditional Indian elements, set in a rural landscape of deep red earth and widespread forestation. The residents are involved in agriculture, administration, commerce and handicrafts, alternative technology, education, healthcare and development projects. The central Matrimandir is not a temple but a place for individual silent meditation. Soil from 124 countries has been placed in a lotus-shaped urn and mixed to symbolize universal oneness. This urn is today sited at the centre of an Amphitheatre in the Matrimandir Gardens . The Matrimandirs 12-sided white marble Inner Chamber has an optical-quality glass globe at its centre, onto which a shaft of sunlight is focused by way of a roof-mounted heliostat. The light falling on the globe acts as a focal aid to concentration.

This temple dedicated to Ganesha is more than three hundred years old. It has a golden spire and walls portraying forty different forms of Ganesha. The temple also has a smaller shrine dedicated to Lord Murugan, who is Ganeshas younger brother. Over five thousand devotees flock to this site everyday. The temple compound also plays host to Lakshmi, the temple elephant, who uses her trunk to dispense blessings and to collect coins from the devotees.

Believed to be the oldest temple in town, dating back to 600 CE, this temple built in the typical Dravidian style, complete with brightly coloured gopuram and sculpted pillars, is probably the oldest standing structure in Puducherry. This temple is dedicated to Lord Vishnu. Legend has it, that the temple was originally built for the idols of Rama, Sita, Lakshman and Hanuman, which were brought to the present site by fishermen, from the sea. The main deity here is Venkatachalapathy (Vishnu). Right behind that is a separate shrine for Narasimha (who is also an incarnation of Vishnu).

This temple, dedicated to the godess Shakti is unique as it seems to be strongly influenced by the French architectural style. It has an unusual blend of both Tamil and French architecture. With its arched walls, ionic columns, stained glass windows and even some angel decorations, it is reminiscent of a French building. However, the inner ceiling supported by the more traditional granite pillars and the sanctum sanctorum, which has a typical Tamil design, highlights the more traditional Tamil features.

Name/Title: Église Notre Dame des Anges (Our Lady of Angels Church)
Description: A gothic and baroque architectural gem built in 1855, mimicking the Lourdes Basilica. Also known as the White Chapel, it's the only church in the world where prayers resonate in French, Tamil, and English.
Built in 1938 as an ode to soldiers who lost their lives during World War I, standing on Goubert Avenue to honor their valour.

The Puducherry museum is located in the former residence of the French administrator building. The museum has a collection of rare bronzes and stone sculptures from the Pallava and Chola dynasties and artifacts excavated from Arikamedu, including remnants of Greek and Roman jars, two hundred year old beads made from glass and precious stones and even objects from the Tsung period in China. The museum also has a Geology room, a shell and fossil room and a collection of handicrafts, coins, church relics and French furniture. Aayi Mandapam, is a shining white monument built during the time of Napoleon III, Emperor of the France. The monument commemorates both the provision of water to the French city during his reign and the good deed of Aayi, - a sixteenth century courtesan, who razed down her home and replaced it with a reservoir. To appease a passing king, angry at having mistaken her candle-lit residence for a holy place. It was from this lake that Napoleon's men quenched their thirst, some three hundred years later. Napoleon, charmed by the story, ordered a monument to be built in Greco-Roman architecture, during the reign of Napoleon III-Emperor of France. It bears the name of Aayi.

Description: The white and brown neo-gothic church is one of Puducherrys finest Catholic churches. It was built by French missionaries in the 1700s in a contrasting Neo-Gothic manner, with towers flanking a central gable and stained glass windows on the side. The church has an imposing entrance and the beautiful stained glass panels depict incidents from Jesus Christs life. Further along the southern boulevard is the cemetery which has some interesting tombs with ornate marble decorations.

Name/Title: Puducherry- Handicrafts- Applique and Patch Work
Description: The word applique is a French term. It is a technique where in several pieces of coloured fabrics are superimposed in patches to give a decorative effect. The patches are then sewn to the base fabric to give specific form and design. In Puducherry during festival processions these are usually found on the temple chariots for covering the horizontal beams. Applique work is also done on long tubular pieces which look like long pillars hanging down the sides of the chariots. Usually these are made of cotton and depict images of Durga, Shiva, Ganesha and Kartikeya in bright vibrant shades of red, white, black, blue and yellow.
Hand-tool etching on leather is done in Auroville in Puducherry. The terracotta coloured leather is etched and braided by hand, and then coloured in two main colours, tan and brown mixed with black.

Name/Title: Puducherry- Handicrafts- Wire Toys and Puzzles
Description: Toy-making is a handicraft in Puducherry. Shell toys consist of large individual shells or small ones stuck together to form an animal or a human figure. Homemade toys in this region are made of leaves, fruit skin like pomegranate skin, twigs, paper and wire. Vahanas or vehicles made of wood on wheels are usually pull-along toys for the child or many also be used as walkers for toddlers.
Local handloom
Local artisans famously create woven dining mats, candles, incense sticks, screen paintings, and intricate batik paintings on cloth, fusing French and Tamil traditions.

The Golden Temple or Darbar Sahib in Amritsar is the most sacred place for the Sikhs. It represents the magnificence of the Sikhs all over the world. Also known as Harminder Sahib, it is a great example of the spirit of tolerance and acceptance that the Sikh philosophy promotes. In the architecture of the Golden temple are included symbols associated with places of worship of other religions. Sri Harminder Sahib is built on a 67ft. square platform in the centre of a Sarovar (tank). The Golden temple has entrances from all the four sides. The temple is within a square pillared enclosure. Within the enclosed complex there is a massive square known as amritsar, or pool of nectar, from which the city derives its name. A marble ambulatory with white, black, and ochre stone tiles forming geometric designs surrounds the pool of water. The main square shrine stands on a platform in the centre of the pool. This shrine is approached through the Darshan Deorhi which is a richly inlaid marble archway on the northeast side. The doors of the archway are covered with silver and ivory, and the upper portions of the shrine are made of gold-plated copper sheets with embossed designs and sacred verses. A marble passage with gilded lamps along the sides, leads to a central hall with four silver doors in the cardinal directions and marble steps, called Har ki Pauri which descends into the water on the southern side. The Sheesh Mahal on the second floor is embellished mostly with floral designs made of coloured and mirrored glass, and semi precious stones inlaid in marble. It was in the nineteenth century, during the reign of Maharaja Ranjit Singh, that the people lavished their wealth on the Golden temple. The Guru Granth Sahib, the holy book of the Sikhs, was installed in the Harmandir Sahib in 1604.

Name/Title: Punjab- Monument- Mausoleums of Ustad and Shagird, Jalandhar
Description: 1600-1650 Medieval Two beautiful seventeenth century tombs are situated in Nakodar belonging to Ustad (teacher) Mohammed Momin Hussaini alias Hafizah, a musician in the service of Khan-e-Khana- the chamberlain of Emperor Jahangir. The other tomb belongs to Haji Jamal, his disciple. The mausoleums are similar in architecture to Emperor Humayuns tomb in Delhi and stand out as buildings of great magnificence.

Sarai Nurmahal, a small town around thirteen kilometer from Jalandhar is linked with Nurjahan, wife of Emperor Jahangir, Mughal Sarai alias Sarai Nurmahal, was constructed for Nurjahan, who was known for her beauty and style of living. It is a remarkable example of Islamic architecture. Its massive gate embellished with arches, filigree work and tiles of beautiful patterns is topped by 4 delicate minarets.

Some festivals are held in the Punjab in honour of the Sikh Gurus. These are called Gurupurabs. They are well spread over the year. There are three important Gurupurabs. On the full moon of Kartik  in November, the birth anniversary of Guru Nanak is celebrated by the devotees with great ardour. Two days earlier a non-stop reading of the Adi Granth is started. At different places religious congregations are held and hymns from the Granth Sahib are chanted. Large processions are taken out through the towns. At night buildings are illuminated. The birth anniversary of Guru Gobind Singh is also celebrated in a similar manner. The third important Gurupurab is the one associated with the martyrdom of Guru Arjun Dev.

Lohri marks the culmination of winter, and is celebrated in the month of Paush or Magh, a day before Makar Sankranti on thirteenth of January. It is a popular harvest festival of Punjab. People get together in groups around a bonfire and sing and dance.

Baisakhi is a seasonal festival celebrated all over the state at the time when harvest is gathered in and the farmer revels in the fulfillment of his years hard work. Since this festival is also an expression of prosperity, singing and dancing constitute its most enchanting features.

The Punjabs famous dances, Bhangra and Giddha are inextricably linked with this festival. Bhangra is a lively form of music and dance. People traditionally perform Bhangra when celebrating the harvest. This dance is performed on Baisakhi when harvesting is over and fairs are held. During Bhangra, people sing Punjabi Boliyaan - lyrics, at least one person plays the the dhol drum, and other people may play the flute, dholak, or other musical instruments. While Bhangra began as a part of harvest festival celebrations, it eventually became a part of such diverse occasions as weddings and New Year celebrations.

Kikli is generally popular with the younger girls. They form pairs and then the two girls of each pair stand opposite each other holding each others hands crosswise. Then they lift their heels and swing round and round on their toes.

Craft forms an integral part of the lifestyle of the people of Punjab. Phulkari, is an art of embroidering shawls, dupattas with floral motifs, dress materials etc. It is done on handspun, handwoven coarse dyed khadi with an ordinary needle and strands of untwisted silk. It is a skillful art of a single stitch that provides interesting patterns on the cloth. The smaller the stitch, finer is the quality of the embroidery. The silk threads in golden yellow, red, crimson, orange, green, blue, and pink are usually employed for the embroidery. The notable aspect of this technique is that single strand was used at a time, each part worked in one color and the varied color effect is obtained by clever use of horizontal, vertical or diagonal stitches. In Phulkari the design is worked very closely that even a square inch of the base cloth is not visible. It is then called Bagh. Besides floral motifs, birds, animals, human figures, vegetables, pots, buildings, rivers, the sun and the moon, scenes of village life, and other imagery are embroidered. Some of the designs include dhaniya bagh (coriander garden), motia bagh (jasmine garden), satranga bagh (garden of rainbow), leheria bagh (garden of waves) and many other depictions. It is made by female members of the house, and takes a long time to make; sometimes even a few years. Traditionally, a Phulkari shawl is gifted to the daughter at her wedding. Another kind of shawl is the Chope, It is very simple in comparison to the Phulkari and Bagh, and is presented to a new bride by her maternal grandmother. The darshan dwar shawl is gifted to a temple by a devotee whose wish has been fulfilled.

At Kartarpur, Jalandhar and Hoshiarpur, craftsmen create pidhis which are low, four-legged woven stools. They are carved out from wood, and then covered with lacquer and woven with threads of different colors. Other lacquer ware products include table lamps and dolls. Motifs and ornamentation are drawn from life around them -Patta (leaf), dodi (bud), jhari (bush), flowers and animals and birds-are some of the common ones.

Leather jootis (shoes and slippers) of Punjab are extremely well known. Rich gold and multi-colored threads are used to decorate and impart a royal touch to a variety of jootis crafted from leather of different shades. In many parts of Punjab, entire families continue to devote themselves to making jootis.
